arcticSedimentCarbon.fieldHasNoDecadeFilter: The interpolated field is supplied ready-made by CASCADE and carries no time axis, so a decade filter cannot act on it. Switch to Stations to filter by decade.

miningConcessions.label: Mining Concessions
miningConcessions.updateFreq: Updated when ISA publishes new contracts — typically yearly
miningConcessions.description: Active ISA exploration contract areas granted to states and companies. Each polygon is one contract block. Clicking a block shows the contractor, resource type, contract area, and expiry date.
miningConcessions.reading: Cyan = active concession. The block boundary is the ISA-approved exploration zone. Area (km²) and expiry date in the popup tell you whether a contract is still valid.
miningConcessions.colorStandard: Outline cyan = platform convention (do-not-change). Resource fills follow FGDC commodity colors (USGS NGMDB).

relinquishedAreas.label: Relinquished Areas
relinquishedAreas.updateFreq: Updated as contracts are terminated or expire
relinquishedAreas.description: Former contract blocks that have been handed back to the ISA — the mining company abandoned them or the contract lapsed. These areas may still contain valuable deposits.
relinquishedAreas.reading: Red dashed outline = no longer under contract. The 'Relinquished by' note in the popup shows who held the contract.

reservedAreas.label: Reserved Areas
reservedAreas.source: ISA — Areas Reserved for Developing States
reservedAreas.updateFreq: Rarely changes; set by ISA Council
reservedAreas.description: Sections of the seabed set aside by the ISA under the 'parallel system', where developing countries may apply for contracts. Not yet under active exploitation.
reservedAreas.reading: Green = reserved but uncontracted. No active mining planned.

apeis.label: Protected Areas (APEIs)
apeis.description: Areas of Particular Environmental Interest: 9 zones in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone and similar designations elsewhere where mining is permanently prohibited to protect representative ecosystems.
apeis.reading: Purple = no mining permitted. These are the strongest legal protections available for deep-sea ecosystems.

obisSpecies.label: OBIS Species (Deep)
obisSpecies.source: Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS) (25 March 2025) OBIS Occurrence Data. Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO. https://doi.org/10.25607/obis.occurrence.b89117cd. Loaded from the OBIS Open Data parquet archive on AWS (s3://obis-open-data/occurrence/, GeoParquet, ~50 GB, ~6,900 files). Conservation status from IUCN Red List via GBIF.
obisSpecies.updateFreq: Full deep-sea snapshot ingested from OBIS Open Data; IUCN categories enriched via GBIF
obisSpecies.description: OBIS Open Data occurrences for the deep-sea species this layer tracks, at a depth floor of 50 m — corals excepted, and see the selection criteria below for exactly what that means. At low zoom, dots are grid cells summarising hundreds or thousands of observations, coloured by conservation threat level; at zoom 8 and above, individual species points appear. Dot colour is IUCN Red List status: red = Critically Endangered or Endangered, orange = Vulnerable, green = not threatened.
obisSpecies.reading: Red dot = area with CR or EN species. Orange dot = Vulnerable species present. Green dot = no IUCN-threatened species. At high zoom, click a dot to see species name, IUCN status, taxonomy, and image. The 'RISK' badge on mining concessions triggers when threatened species overlap the claim area.
obisSpecies.colorStandard: IUCN Red List palette — CR/EN crimson, VU amber, NT yellow, LC blue (iucnredlist.org).
obisSpecies.selectionCriteria: We include an occurrence if and only if all of: (1) depth ≥ 50 m — a floor that excludes intertidal/surface noise while keeping continental-shelf (50–500 m, offshore-claim relevant) and deep-sea records; curation to deep-sea-relevant taxa happens at the species-list level, not via the depth cut; (2) OBIS quality flags pass — `dropped` IS NOT TRUE and `absence` IS NOT TRUE, so withdrawn records and 'species was searched for and NOT found' rows are excluded; (3) georeferenced — `interpreted.decimalLatitude` and `interpreted.decimalLongitude` are present; (4) has a WoRMS-validated `interpreted.scientificName` and a stable OBIS `_id`. Everything else is in. (5) the scientific name is one this layer already tracks — the sync filters the OBIS archive by `SELECT DISTINCT scientific_name FROM biodiversity_hotspots`, so it looks for the species it already holds. ⚠️ The consequence, in the ingest's own words: that list, being derived from this very table, can never learn a species the depth floor had already excluded. Corals are the deliberate exception — matched by taxonomic ORDER and FAMILY at any depth, precisely to break that closure for reef-building Scleractinia, which live almost entirely above 50 m. So this is not an unfiltered mirror of OBIS: it is OBIS as seen through a species list that grows only when something else adds to it.
obisSpecies.limitations: Depth comes from `interpreted.minimumDepthInMeters` — records with no reported depth are excluded even if collected from deep water (a known gap for older expedition logs). Coordinate precision varies by dataset (some are degree-rounded ship tracks). IUCN status is only available for the small subset of species formally assessed by the Red List; most deep-sea taxa are Data Deficient or unassessed and render in the neutral palette.

seamounts.label: Seamounts
seamounts.source: Yesson, C. et al. (2020) List of seamounts in the world oceans — An update [dataset]. PANGAEA, https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.921688 (37,889 seamounts, SRTM v.11 bathymetry).
seamounts.updateFreq: Static 2020 dataset — imported from PANGAEA on demand
seamounts.description: 37,889 submarine mountains (height ≥ 1,000 m) identified from SRTM v.11 global bathymetry. Updated from the 2011 catalogue with ~4,400 newly discovered seamounts. They concentrate biodiversity and are targets for cobalt-rich ferromanganese crust mining. Yellow columns mark features inside concession areas.
seamounts.reading: Blue column = outside any contract. Yellow column = inside a mining concession. Click a seamount to see height, summit depth, base area, size class, and whether it was newly discovered in the 2020 update.
seamounts.limitations: Based on 15-arc-second SRTM bathymetry. Some features along ridges may be artifacts of complex topography. Only ~20% of the ocean floor has been mapped by direct sonar survey.

argoFloats.label: Argo Floats
argoFloats.updateFreq: Synced daily; profiles typically transmitted every 10 days per float
argoFloats.description: Autonomous ocean profiling floats measuring temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen from surface to 2,000 m. Red floats have at least one anomalous sensor reading — low oxygen, low pH, or temperature/salinity outside the dataset's normal range. Use the Alarm Filters tab to show only floats with specific anomaly types.
argoFloats.reading: Cyan 3D column = Argo float with normal readings. Red column = float with at least one alarm (low oxygen, low pH, or temp/salinity anomaly). Amber ring around a float = pH above 8.6, which is physically impossible in seawater and flagged as a likely sensor fault — its popup shows the value struck through with a red "sensor fault" tag. Column height encodes the float's maximum dive depth — taller = deeper profile. Lime-green trail = normal float path; red trail = alarmed float path. After tracking plumes, trail dots become clickable — tap one to see depth, temperature, and salinity at that historical position.

hydrothermalVents.label: Hydrothermal Vents
hydrothermalVents.source: Beaulieu, S.E. & Szafrański, K.M. (2020) InterRidge Global Database of Active Submarine Hydrothermal Vent Fields Version 3.4 [dataset]. PANGAEA, https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.917894
hydrothermalVents.updateFreq: Frozen. Version 3.4 was completed 25 March 2020 and no newer version exists — InterRidge's own live database does not respond.
hydrothermalVents.description: Vent fields from the InterRidge global database. Active vents InterRidge's own survey confirmed by direct observation are shown as tall red 3D spikes with a red glow halo; active vents InterRidge only inferred from a plume or chemical anomaly (not directly observed) get the same height and colour, dimmer, with no glow. Inactive vents appear as shorter grey columns. Vents inside Polymetallic Sulphide concession areas are flagged as conflicts in the claim popup.
hydrothermalVents.reading: Tall red spike + red glow = active, confirmed by direct observation. Tall red spike, dimmer, no glow = active, only inferred from a plume or anomaly. Short grey column = inactive. Spike and column size scales with zoom. Click a vent to see: depth range, max temperature, ocean & region, tectonic setting, national jurisdiction, discovery year, full spreading rate, other published names, and biology notes (species observed). ChEssBase species within 5 km are listed if available. Vent–mining conflicts are listed in the Mining Concession popup when you click an affected claim.
hydrothermalVents.limitations: 721 vent fields, 666 active and 55 inactive, as the source counts them. Three limits matter when reading this layer. First, the data stop at 25 March 2020: fields described since then are absent, and at least four are known from other compilations — Jøtul on the Knipovich Ridge, Old City on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Yaeyama Knoll and Macauley Volcano. Second, a vent field is an area, not a chimney; one marker can stand for dozens of chimneys. Third, the compilers state their database is not comprehensive for inactive fields, so the 55 is what has been documented, not what exists.

eezBoundaries.label: EEZ Boundaries
eezBoundaries.source: Marine Regions — World EEZ v12 (Flanders Marine Institute, 2023)
eezBoundaries.updateFreq: Re-synced every 30 days; boundaries change only when states renegotiate or dispute resolution occurs
eezBoundaries.description: Exclusive Economic Zones — the 200 nautical mile (370 km) maritime jurisdictions extending from each coastal state's baseline. Within an EEZ, the coastal state has sovereign rights over all natural resources including seabed minerals. ISA contracts can only operate in areas beyond national jurisdiction (the 'Area'), so EEZ boundaries define where ISA authority ends and national law begins.
eezBoundaries.reading: Gold dashed outline = EEZ boundary. Clicking anywhere inside a zone shows the country name, sovereign state, ISO code, and zone area. The 'Jurisdiction' field in Mining Concession popups will say 'Inside [Country] EEZ' if the claim falls within a national zone, or 'International Waters / ISA' if it sits in the Area. All current ISA contracts should fall outside EEZ zones; any overlap would be a legal anomaly.

unescoMarineHeritage.label: UNESCO Marine Heritage
unescoMarineHeritage.source: Marine Regions — UNESCO World Heritage Marine Programme (via MarineRegions.org WFS)
unescoMarineHeritage.updateFreq: Re-synced every 30 days; UNESCO designations change rarely
unescoMarineHeritage.description: UNESCO World Heritage Marine Programme sites — internationally recognised marine protected areas of Outstanding Universal Value. These sites receive the highest level of international recognition under the 1972 World Heritage Convention. Mining claims within 200 km of a UNESCO site are flagged with a 'High Sensitivity' badge in the claim popup.
unescoMarineHeritage.reading: Green outline = UNESCO World Heritage marine site. Clicking the polygon shows the site name and country. The 200 km proximity threshold used for the 'High Sensitivity' warning is a precautionary buffer — UNESCO sites themselves do not extend 200 km, but potential sediment plumes and current-borne disturbance from deep-sea mining can travel that distance.

noiseRiskGrid.label: Noise Risk Grid
noiseRiskGrid.source: ICES Registry (gis.ices.dk) — impulsive noise PBD; EMODnet Physics (funded by EC DG MARE, CC BY 4.0) — continuous SPL; OBIS-SEAMAP (seamap.env.duke.edu) — cetacean sightings
noiseRiskGrid.updateFreq: Recomputed when ingestion scripts run (quarterly target)
noiseRiskGrid.description: Per-cell Impact Risk Index combining underwater noise intensity with cetacean presence and IUCN conservation status. MODELED, not observed. Formula: (pbd_norm or spl_norm) × cetacean_norm × species_weight, capped at 1.0 (MSFD Descriptor 11 methodology). pbd_norm (pulse-block days, ICES/EMODnet INER) and spl_norm (continuous SPL, EMODnet) are two independent noise measures that are never blended into one figure — each cell carries whichever one its source measured. Covers OSPAR/HELCOM/Baltic regions (ICES) and global monitoring stations (EMODnet). Cells with noise data but no cetacean survey coverage are marked as 'data gap' — absence of records does not mean absence of animals.
noiseRiskGrid.reading: Red = Critical (≥0.8). Orange = High (0.6–0.8). Yellow = Moderate (0.4–0.6). Green = Low (0.2–0.4). Grey = Minimal. Purple = Data gap (high noise, no cetacean survey). Dot size scales with risk index. Click any dot for the full index breakdown including cetacean sighting count, threatened species, and noise source.
noiseRiskGrid.colorStandard: ColorBrewer 2.0 YlOrRd sequential ramp + neutral purple data-gap (colorbrewer2.org).

oceansitesMoorings.label: OceanSITES Moorings
oceansitesMoorings.source: OceanOPS REST API (oceanops.org, CC-BY) · NOAA NDBC · NOAA PMEL ERDDAP (TAO/TRITON/PIRATA/RAMA) · OceanSITES GDAC (IFREMER)
oceansitesMoorings.updateFreq: Station positions synced weekly from OceanOPS; observations refreshed daily, and only for stations OceanOPS currently lists as operational
oceansitesMoorings.description: Fixed deep-ocean mooring stations from the international OceanSITES network. Moorings measure temperature, salinity, currents and biogeochemistry over multi-year timescales — the backbone of deep-sea climate monitoring. The map shows the whole OceanOPS register, roughly 1,070 stations, of which only about 60 are currently operational; the rest are closed, inactive or merely registered and are kept because a decommissioned mooring is still where a long baseline was measured. Live readings are fetched for operational stations only, so most rings carry position and metadata but no measurement. Moorings within 500 km of a mining concession appear in the claim popup.
oceansitesMoorings.reading: Cyan ring = a mooring in the OceanSITES/OceanOPS register. Click for station code, network, deployment date and, where a feed exists, cached readings together with the source that supplied them — NDBC, PMEL ERDDAP or the OceanSITES GDAC. A ring with no readings is not a failure: we only poll currently operational moorings, and in practice the readings come from PMEL and the GDAC rather than NDBC. Proximity to mining claims indicates that long-term scientific baselines could be disrupted by sediment plumes or seismic noise.

oceanCurrents.label: Ocean Currents
oceanCurrents.updateFreq: Baked daily from Copernicus Marine; ~6 months of daily history retained
oceanCurrents.description: Animated flow of ocean currents from the Copernicus Marine global physical analysis/forecast. Switch the depth selector between Surface and 1000 m — the 1000 m field is the water mass that carries deep-sea mining sediment plumes. A date slider with playback shows the daily current field for any day in the past ~6 months.
oceanCurrents.reading: Particle streaks follow current direction; brighter/warmer streaks mean faster flow. Use the depth toggle to compare surface drift against the deeper plume-bearing layer. With reduced motion enabled the field renders as static arrows.
oceanCurrents.limitations: Daily snapshot, downsampled to ~0.5° — not real-time and not eddy-resolving. Direction and speed are indicative, not navigational. Historical days are daily-mean snapshots; the most recent ~6 months come from the CMEMS near-real-time analysis.

oncObservatories.label: ONC Observatories
oncObservatories.source: Ocean Networks Canada — Oceans 3.0 API (data.oceannetworks.ca, CC BY 4.0)
oncObservatories.updateFreq: Locations synced weekly from ONC API; CTD/oxygen sensor readings cached daily — only the 195 stations with verified readings within the past year are shown
oncObservatories.description: Ocean Networks Canada cabled seafloor observatory nodes — permanent underwater infrastructure transmitting real-time seismic, pressure, temperature, salinity, and chemistry data via subsea cable. ONC operates NEPTUNE (NE Pacific, depths to 2,660 m) and VENUS (coastal BC) networks, plus Arctic and Atlantic nodes. Unlike Argo floats, these are fixed in place. The map covers ONC's whole location tree, not only the cabled nodes — drifting buoys and instruments from finished expeditions are included, and the latest reading held for one of those may be years old. Note: NE Pacific has no active ISA mining claims (all seamounts and vent fields are protected under the ThT MPA framework).
oncObservatories.reading: Teal glow dot = ONC observatory with verified sensor data. Click for station name, depth, and cached daily readings (temperature, salinity, pressure, oxygen where available). Use the EOV filter (+) to narrow both this layer and ONC Instruments to a specific Essential Ocean Variable: Currents (ADCP/current meters), Ocean sound (hydrophones), Oxygen (CTDs/O₂ sensors), or Particulate matter (turbidity/fluorometry). EOVs follow the GOOS/CIOOS taxonomy.

chemosynthenticSites.label: Chemosynthetic Sites
chemosynthenticSites.source: Ramirez-Llodra E (2025). ChEssBase. Version 1.0. Flanders Marine Institute. Occurrence dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/6v6ug8 accessed via GBIF.org.
chemosynthenticSites.updateFreq: Synced weekly from the ChEssBase dataset on GBIF (datasetKey: dc5abc9f-84d5-4046-a3ef-9ab24ae53756). Citation accessed-on date is the date of the most recent successful sync.
chemosynthenticSites.description: Cold seeps, whale falls, and oxygen-minimum zones from ChEssBase — the global database of chemosynthetic ecosystem species. These habitats support life through chemical energy rather than sunlight: seeps release methane and hydrogen sulfide, whale falls become transient oases, and OMZs host unique low-oxygen adapted communities. Dots are grouped by named locality; one dot = one site, which may have dozens of species records. Vent-classified ChEssBase records are merged into the Hydrothermal Vents layer instead of appearing here.
chemosynthenticSites.reading: Teal dot = Cold Seep. Pink dot = Whale Fall. Periwinkle dot = OMZ / Other. Click any dot for site name, depth range, species count, phyla breakdown, and expandable species list. Use the habitat + phylum filters (+ button) to focus on specific ecosystem or taxonomic groups. Chemosynthetic sites near mining claims raise the claim's risk score — see 'Chemosynthetic Ecosystem Proximity' in the claim popup.
chemosynthenticSites.colorStandard: ColorBrewer 2.0 Set2 qualitative palette — colors do not rank (colorbrewer2.org).

contractorStations.label: Contractor Sampling Stations
contractorStations.source: Platform-derived analysis from ISA DeepData via OBIS-hosted DwC archives (datasets.obis.org/hosted/isa/)
contractorStations.updateFreq: Synced weekly via incremental HEAD probes (ETag/Last-Modified). Steady-state bandwidth ≈ 0; only changed/new archives are downloaded.
contractorStations.description: Physical sampling deployments aggregated from the 140 contractor DwC archives that ISA mirrors through OBIS. Each dot = one Multi-Corer / Box-Corer / Epibenthic Sledge / CTD station, color-coded by contractor (NORI, UKSRL, BGR, IFREMER, COMRA, …). The companion DeepData layer in Baseline Monitoring Density shows the raw occurrence records 1:1 from OBIS REST; this layer is the platform's own station-level rollup, useful for visualising who is monitoring where.
contractorStations.reading: Pink dot = NORI (Nauru-sponsored). Magenta dot = TOML (Tonga-sponsored). Amber = BGR (Germany). Blue = IFREMER (France). Sky = UKSRL. Red = COMRA (China). Cyan = Korea. Violet = JOGMEC (Japan). Click any dot for sampling protocol, depth, sediment horizons (parsed from eventID), occurrence count, distinct species count, and the contractor's verbatim citation + license. Use the contractor filter (+) to narrow to specific operators — empty selection shows everyone.
contractorStations.limitations: Platform-aggregated analysis, not raw contractor records. The verbatim eventID is shown in every panel for full audit traceability back to the source DwC archive. Sediment horizon parsing is best-effort and follows the NORI/TOML 'L_min_max' naming scheme; other contractors may show no horizon information even when sub-core data exists. ~1,400 occurrences across 21 archives carry no parseable contractor code — these appear under the '(unparsed)' chip in the contractor filter and render as slate-grey dots. Toggle the chip to isolate them.
contractorStations.colorStandard: Distinct hues per contractor, hand-picked for color-blind separability and (where intuitive) sponsor-state association.

submarineCables.label: Submarine Cables
submarineCables.source: EMODnet Human Activities (funded by EC DG MARE, CC BY 4.0) + Ocean Networks Canada + OOI (NSF) + NOAA Marine Cadastre (coast.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/Hosted/SubmarineCables/FeatureServer/0)
submarineCables.updateFreq: EMODnet weekly, ONC monthly, OOI quarterly, NOAA quarterly
submarineCables.description: Six complementary cable datasets in one layer. **EMODnet** = 7 aggregated contributor layers (~1,260 features across European waters): Norway NVE power cables (918), Dutch Rijkswaterstaat telecom + power (135 combined), German BSH telecom + power (117 combined), UK fibre optic (30), Spain IGN + Atlantic terminations (60). Includes named interconnectors like NORNED (Norway↔Netherlands) and Baltic Cable (Germany↔Sweden); operator names, voltage where applicable, and installation years available for most power cables. **NOAA Marine Cadastre** (joint NOAA/BOEM) = 2,816 US cable corridors as polygon outlines (legally-protected anchoring-prohibited zones, not centerlines; includes ~371 Great Lakes cables alongside marine routes). **LINZ** = New Zealand chart-symbology cable lines in the NZ EEZ, sourced from Land Information NZ hydrographic charts; route geometries are present but operator names and system identifiers are not encoded in chart data. **ACMA** = three federal Submarine Cable Protection Zones (Sydney North, Sydney South, Perth) where anchoring, trawling, and seabed disturbance are prohibited under Australian law. **ONC** = fibre-optic observatory backbone (NEPTUNE + VENUS) powering live seafloor sensors off British Columbia. **OOI** = Regional Cabled Array (Pacific City, OR → Axial Seamount + Newport loop), the only US deep-sea cabled observatory — approximate routes from authoritative node coordinates. Expand the row to toggle sources independently.\n\nWhere the layer still goes silent — Canadian Atlantic coastal waters, the deep mid-Atlantic, the remaining Baltic gap (Swedish, Finnish, Danish, Polish and Baltic-state internal waters; German BSH and Norway NVE now cover much of the western/northern Baltic), and most non-Anglophone hydrographic EEZs — reflects an institutional gap rather than missing cables. Canada's Hydrographic Service (CHS) holds Crown copyright on its chart data and licences distribution per dataset, so it isn't republished here; deep international waters have no government registry because UNCLOS grants the right to lay cables there without a registration mandate; and most non-Anglophone hydrographic offices either restrict redistribution or publish only paper charts. The 2024 ITU/ICPC Submarine Cable Resilience Initiative is the first multilateral effort to address this — currently policy-focused, not yet a public data layer.
submarineCables.reading: Amber line = EMODnet telecom cable or NOAA Marine Cadastre corridor outline (US). Cyan line = ONC observatory cable. Magenta line = OOI RCA backbone (approximate). Click any for name/status/length. Cables near mining concessions highlight infrastructure risk.

oncInstruments.label: ONC Instruments
oncInstruments.description: Individual scientific instruments deployed on Ocean Networks Canada's cabled observatory off Canada's west coast. Each point is one device — CTDs, hydrophones, cameras, oxygen sensors, accelerometers, junction boxes — with live power and data via the ONC fibre-optic backbone. Dense clustering on the Endeavour Ridge and Barkley Canyon corresponds to their observatory nodes. The EOV filter on ONC Observatories also applies here.
oncInstruments.reading: Violet dot = one instrument. Click for device category, model, code, host location, depth, and image when available. EOV filter (on ONC Observatories row): Currents = all ADCP variants + Current Meter; Ocean sound = Hydrophone, Acoustic Receiver, Bioacoustic Echosounder; Oxygen = Oxygen Sensor, CTD, Integrated CTD pH O2; Particulate matter = Fluorometer, Turbidity Meter, CDOM.

portLocations.label: Port Locations
portLocations.description: Global port infrastructure. Ports are the logistical backbone of any offshore mining operation — equipment staging, ore transport, and supply chain routing all funnel through port facilities.
portLocations.reading: Blue ⚓ = port. Click for city, state/region, and country. Proximity to mining concessions indicates potential staging or transport hubs.

tectonicPlates.label: Tectonic Plates
tectonicPlates.source: Peter Bird (2003) via PANGAEA — public domain
tectonicPlates.description: Global tectonic plate boundaries and polygons from Peter Bird's 2003 model. Plate boundaries are where hydrothermal vents cluster, oceanic crust forms, and seismic risk concentrates — directly relevant to mining site selection and risk assessment.
tectonicPlates.reading: Subtle sandstone fill = plate area. Copper line = plate boundary. Click for plate name or boundary type (divergent, convergent, transform). Boundary lines near mining concessions indicate elevated seismic and geological risk.

monitoringDensity.label: Baseline Monitoring Density
monitoringDensity.source: Derived from 15 sources: OBIS (hotspot_grid), ChEssBase, Argo floats, OceanSITES moorings, ONC instruments, WOD/NOAA (CTD + bottle station coordinates), PANGAEA (research cruise datasets), BCO-DMO (US NSF ocean chemistry + biology cruises), NOAA DataCite (ocean survey datasets), OBIS-SEAMAP (cetacean and pinniped occurrences), CCHDO / GO-SHIP (repeat hydrography cruise tracks), SIO Benthic Invertebrate Collection (Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego), ISA DeepData (contractor environmental reports via OBIS), MBARI VARS (Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute deep-sea ROV via OBIS), and NOAA Deep-Sea Coral & Sponge (NOAA DSCRTP — corals + sponges via NOAA ArcGIS, ~1.5M records, mostly >200 m) — aggregated internally
monitoringDensity.updateFreq: Aggregated every 12h; underlying source tables refresh on their own cadence (Argo 12h, ONC daily, most others weekly).
monitoringDensity.description: Each cell is an equal-area hexagon (~48,760 km², EPSG:6933) coloured by the number of baseline scientific monitoring records within it, drawn from fifteen data sources: OBIS pre-aggregated hotspot grid, ChEssBase chemosynthetic sites, Argo float profiles, OceanSITES fixed moorings, ONC instruments, NOAA World Ocean Database (WOD) CTD/bottle station coordinates, PANGAEA research cruise datasets (including GEOTRACES trace-element baselines), BCO-DMO US NSF ocean chemistry and biology cruises, NOAA DataCite ocean survey records, OBIS-SEAMAP cetacean/pinniped occurrences, CCHDO / GO-SHIP repeat hydrography cruise tracks, the SIO Benthic Invertebrate Collection (Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego — deep-sea museum specimens, used by permission of C. Seid 2026), ISA DeepData contractor environmental reports (mirrored via OBIS, 201k records), MBARI VARS deep-sea ROV observations (mirrored via OBIS, 175k records), and NOAA Deep-Sea Coral & Sponge (NOAA DSCRTP — corals + sponges, ~1.5M records, mostly >200 m). Colour scale by records per cell: cream = 0–4 (monitoring gap), yellow = 5–19 (sparse), orange = 20–59 (moderate), red = 60–199 (good coverage), dark red = 200+ (well-observed). More records = darker = stronger baseline coverage; pale cells are potential monitoring gaps. Inspired by ONC scientist feedback (Dwight, April 2026): toggle alongside Mining Concessions, Reserved Areas, and Relinquished Areas to identify frontline exploitation zones where baseline environmental science is thin. Note: the Contractor Sampling Stations layer, when enabled, shows platform-derived rollups of the same DeepData occurrences already counted here — enabling both layers together does not double-count records in the density calculation. Within the source list, MBARI VARS, NOAA Deep-Sea Coral & Sponge, and ISA DeepData are surfaced separately for naming credit but their records are also reflected in the broader OBIS source; this overlap is intentional and documented per source.
monitoringDensity.reading: Pale cream = fewer records = monitoring gap. Dark red = more records = better baseline coverage. Click any cell to see a per-source breakdown. Blank cells = not in these fifteen databases, not confirmed unmonitored — contractor-held baseline data is not publicly available.

miningFootprints.label: Global Mining Footprints
miningFootprints.source: Maus, V. et al. (2022) Global-scale mining polygons (Version 2) [dataset]. PANGAEA, https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.942325. CC BY 4.0. Derived from Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery at 10m resolution.
miningFootprints.updateFreq: Static dataset — Sentinel-2 derived; no live sync (imported once from PANGAEA)
miningFootprints.description: 74,548 mine polygons (open pits, tailings ponds, waste rock dumps, heap leach pads, and processing plants) mapped globally from Sentinel-2 satellite imagery. This is the most comprehensive open dataset of surface mining extent — covering coal, metals, industrial minerals, and aggregates. Each polygon includes the country, primary commodity (where known), and area in km². The dataset exposes the true spatial footprint of extraction that corporate reporting rarely quantifies.
miningFootprints.reading: Red polygon = mining footprint. Click for country, feature type (pit/tailings/processing), commodity, and area in km². Links: 'Satellite view' opens Google Maps at the polygon's location for aerial imagery. 'Search online' and 'Wikipedia' search by feature type and country — results are contextual (e.g. 'Coal Mine mining Australia') rather than site-specific, since the source data has no individual mine names. Enable the KBA layer simultaneously to identify mines operating inside Key Biodiversity Areas — a direct indicator of regulatory conflict. Zoom in to see individual pit shapes; at low zoom, polygons simplify for performance.
miningFootprints.limitations: Classification is automated from satellite imagery — some false positives exist in barren or urban areas. Only surface mining is captured; underground mines are invisible to satellite detection. Commodity attribution is incomplete for many polygons. Temporal resolution is a single snapshot (2019–2022 composite), not a time series.
miningFootprints.colorStandard: Hot magenta #DC267F — no FGDC standard for surface-mining footprint polygons; chosen to contrast against the KBA palette during overlap analysis.

keyBiodiversityAreas.label: Key Biodiversity Areas
keyBiodiversityAreas.source: BirdLife International / KBA Partnership — World Database of Key Biodiversity Areas (keybiodiversityareas.org). Identified using the IUCN KBA Standard (2016).
keyBiodiversityAreas.updateFreq: Re-synced every 6 months from KBA Partnership; site boundaries are periodically revised as new assessments are published
keyBiodiversityAreas.description: 16,800+ sites identified using globally standardised criteria as the most important places on Earth for the persistence of biodiversity. KBAs are identified based on species threatened with extinction, geographically restricted species, ecological integrity, biological processes (migrations, congregations), and irreplaceability. Unlike protected areas (WDPA), KBA designation is purely scientific — it does not confer legal protection. Many KBAs overlap with mining footprints, revealing extraction in areas of exceptional biological value.
keyBiodiversityAreas.reading: Magenta polygon = KBA boundary. Click for site name, country, KBA status (confirmed/proposed), criteria met, area in km², and designation year. Overlay with Mining Footprints to see how many km² of KBA land are already being mined.
keyBiodiversityAreas.limitations: KBA assessment coverage is uneven — Europe and the Americas are well-assessed; Central Asia and some Pacific island states have gaps. Marine KBAs exist but are better covered by the ocean layers on this platform. KBA boundaries represent the assessment area, not necessarily the full extent of species habitat.

tailingsDams.label: Tailings Dams
tailingsDams.source: Hudson-Edwards, K. et al. (2023) WAPHA global metal mines database (Dryad, doi:10.5061/dryad.j3tx95xmg, CC0) — 11,587 tailings storage facilities served. Global Tailings Portal (GRID-Arendal) fields are withdrawn pending written permission and are not served.
tailingsDams.updateFreq: Static base dataset (Zenodo 2023). Global Tailings Portal enrichment is withdrawn pending permission from GRID-Arendal — no hazard, ownership or specification fields are served.
tailingsDams.description: 11,587 tailings storage facility locations mapped globally. Tailings dams hold the slurry left after ore processing — they are among the most dangerous engineered structures on Earth. This platform previously enriched a subset of dams with hazard ratings, ownership, dam specifications and safety-review answers disclosed via the Global Tailings Portal (GRID-Arendal); those fields were withdrawn on 2026-09-23 pending written permission and are not served, even on the dams they were once attached to. Every facility shown here carries only its WAPHA-sourced name, location and country.
tailingsDams.reading: Dots mark facility locations; every dot shares one colour — hazard ratings are withdrawn (see Limitations). Click for the facility name and country. Enable the Landslides layer to check if dams sit in landslide-prone terrain. Enable Mining Footprints to see associated mine sites. Enable Water Risk to see water stress at the basin level.
tailingsDams.limitations: Hazard rating, ownership, dam specifications and safety-review fields, previously disclosed via the Global Tailings Portal (GRID-Arendal), are withdrawn pending written permission from GRID-Arendal (Michal's decision, 2026-09-23) and are not served — though the underlying rows and columns remain in the database. Every facility shown carries only its WAPHA-sourced name, location and country. Many Chinese facilities appear as '尾矿库' (generic 'tailings pond'). The WAPHA base set is a literature and registry compilation, not a satellite survey. It inherits a small number of non-mining structures from national dam registers — five records by name, e.g. "ELK NECK STATE PARK DAM" and "COLUMBIA LNG MAIN DAM". Country labels on WAPHA records are platform-derived: the source shapefile publishes only a name and a point.
tailingsDams.colorStandard: Single colour for every facility — no hazard rating is served; ratings are withdrawn pending permission from GRID-Arendal.

activeFires.label: Active Fires (FIRMS)
activeFires.source: NASA LANCE FIRMS — Fire Information for Resource Management System. VIIRS (375 m) from three satellites: Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.
activeFires.updateFreq: Synced every 6 hours; NASA processes satellite passes within 3 hours of overpass
activeFires.description: Near-real-time thermal anomaly detections from NASA's VIIRS instrument, pulled from three satellites — Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 — at 375 m resolution, which together give several overpasses a day and resolve smaller, cooler fires than a 1 km sensor can. Each detection carries brightness temperature, fire radiative power (FRP, an indicator of fire intensity), the acquisition date and time in UTC, a confidence level, and the instrument and satellite as NASA labels them.
activeFires.reading: Yellow dot = low-confidence detection. Orange dot = nominal confidence. Red dot = high confidence. Click for the acquisition date and time in UTC, brightness temperature in Kelvin, FRP in MW, and the instrument and satellite exactly as NASA labels them. Enable Mining Footprints to check if fires are burning inside or adjacent to mine sites — this may indicate coal-seam fires, waste burning or land clearing.
activeFires.limitations: Cloud cover blocks satellite detection — fires under thick cloud are missed entirely. Large industrial heat sources such as flares and smelters can register as detections. A detection is one satellite overpass, not a measurement of how long a fire burned.
activeFires.colorStandard: NASA FIRMS confidence convention — yellow (low) → orange (nominal) → red (high).

airQualityStations.label: Air Quality Stations
airQualityStations.source: OpenAQ (openaq.org) — v3 API. Aggregates government-operated reference-grade monitoring stations from national and regional air quality networks worldwide. CC BY 4.0.
airQualityStations.updateFreq: Station locations synced daily; sensor readings refreshed every 2 hours from OpenAQ sensors API
airQualityStations.description: Government air quality monitoring stations measuring PM2.5 (fine particulate matter), PM10, SO₂ (sulphur dioxide), NO₂ (nitrogen dioxide), O₃ (ozone), and CO (carbon monoxide). These are reference-grade instruments — not low-cost sensors — providing legally admissible measurements used for regulatory compliance. Station placement near mining operations provides direct evidence of air quality impacts on surrounding communities. Readings are cached with timestamp so you can see how recent the measurement is.
airQualityStations.reading: Dot color = US EPA AQI for the latest reading at this station, computed across all reported pollutants and showing the worst (EPA convention). Green = Good (0–50), Yellow = Moderate (51–100), Orange = Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups (101–150), Red = Unhealthy (151–200), Purple = Very Unhealthy (201–300), Maroon = Hazardous (301+), Grey = no parseable concentrations. Click for station name, city, country, and per-pollutant readings with units and timestamps. Enable Mining Footprints to find stations downwind of active mines — elevated PM2.5 and PM10 near open-pit mines is a direct health indicator. SO₂ spikes near smelters indicate industrial emissions.
airQualityStations.limitations: Station density varies enormously by country — Europe and North America are well-covered; sub-Saharan Africa and Central Asia have large monitoring gaps. Not all parameters are measured at every station — many only report PM2.5 or PM10. Readings are cached every 2 hours; for real-time monitoring visit the source network directly. Some stations go offline for maintenance and show stale readings. AQI breakpoints assume EPA averaging windows (PM2.5 24h, O3 8h, NO2/SO2 1h, CO 8h), but OpenAQ 'latest' values are instantaneous — the displayed AQI is *indicative*, not regulatory.
airQualityStations.colorStandard: US EPA AQI palette verbatim (airnow.gov/aqi). Worst-pollutant rule: station AQI = max across PM2.5/PM10/O3/NO2/SO2/CO.

landslideCatalog.label: Landslide Catalog
landslideCatalog.source: NASA COOLR — Cooperative Open Online Landslide Repository (coolr.sci.gsfc.nasa.gov). Compiled by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center with citizen science contributions via Landslide Reporter.
landslideCatalog.updateFreq: Dataset updated periodically by NASA; our sync captures cumulative additions
landslideCatalog.description: Global inventory of rainfall-triggered landslides compiled since 2007, combining satellite-detected events, news reports, government disaster agencies, and citizen science observations. Each record includes the event date, landslide type (landslide, mudslide, rockfall, debris flow, lahar, avalanche), trigger mechanism, geographic accuracy, fatality count (where known), and source report. This layer is critical for assessing geotechnical risk at mine sites and tailings dam locations — slope instability near tailings dams is a primary failure trigger.
landslideCatalog.reading: Brown dot = landslide event. Click for date, landslide type, trigger mechanism, country/location description, fatality count, and source confidence. Enable the Tailings Dams layer to find dams in landslide-prone areas — co-location of tailings facilities with historical landslide events is a red flag for dam safety. The Mining Footprints layer shows whether landslides have occurred inside or adjacent to active mine sites, which may indicate slope instability from excavation.
landslideCatalog.limitations: Detection is heavily biased toward populated areas — remote landslides in uninhabited regions are underreported. Pre-2007 events are sparse. Citizen-reported events may have imprecise coordinates. Not all events have fatality data — 'no fatalities reported' may mean 'no information available'. Submarine landslides are not included (those are relevant to deep-sea mining but covered by different datasets).

globalDams.label: Global Dams
globalDams.source: GDW — Global Dam Watch database v1.0 (GDW_barriers_v1_0, 2024-07-24), figshare doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.25988293, CC BY 4.0. Absorbs GOODD and GRanD, which its publishers state will be discontinued.
globalDams.updateFreq: Static — GDW v1.0, released 2024; updated periodically upstream and reloaded here when a new version appears
globalDams.description: 41,145 river barriers and dams worldwide. GDW merges GOODD's satellite-mapped locations with GRanD's engineering records and ICOLD, so unlike the GOODD-only release served here until 2026-09-11 it carries real attributes — name, river, country, height, reservoir capacity, year and use. ⚠️ It is not complete: 10,071 barriers (24.5%) have a name, 15,229 (37%) a year, 9,311 (23%) a height. Country is the only field present on every point.
globalDams.reading: Indigo dot = one barrier. Click for whatever GDW records about it: a name if the source has one, otherwise its GDW identifier. Empty rows mean the source left the field blank — GDW's no-data code (-99) is stored as no value rather than printed as a measurement. What the layer is for is spatial context: which mines sit upstream or downstream of a barrier, since mines depend on water supply and their tailings can contaminate reservoirs below.
globalDams.limitations: Point locations, not dam crest footprints. Three quarters of barriers are unnamed at source and most carry no height or year. Installed capacity is present on only 242 points (0.6%), so this layer cannot be used to total hydropower. The reservoir polygons GDW publishes alongside the barriers are not served here. GDW v1.0 is a 2024 snapshot; dams built or removed since are absent.

globalSurfaceWater.label: Global Surface Water
globalSurfaceWater.source: JRC / European Commission — Global Surface Water Explorer (global-surface-water.appspot.com). Pekel et al. 2016, Nature. Produced from 4.7 million Landsat scenes (1984–2021) at 30m.
globalSurfaceWater.updateFreq: Static raster tiles (1984–2021 composite); dataset is updated by JRC every 1–2 years with new Landsat data
globalSurfaceWater.description: Surface water mapped from 1984 to 2021 at 30 m resolution, from 4.7 million Landsat scenes — the longest continuous satellite record of global surface water. Shows occurrence frequency: how often each 30 m pixel was seen as water over those 37 years. It reveals permanent rivers and lakes, seasonal wetlands, reservoirs that expanded or shrank, and water bodies created by dam construction or mining. ⚠️ It is not a complete inventory of the world's water: at 30 m, streams and ponds below roughly 900 m² are invisible, and the limitations below say where else it thins out.
globalSurfaceWater.reading: Dark blue = permanent water (present >90% of the time). Lighter blue = seasonal or intermittent (present 10–90%). Raster overlay — no click details per pixel. Use alongside Mining Footprints to see whether mines have created artificial water bodies (pit lakes, tailings ponds) or destroyed natural ones. Compare with Dams to see actual reservoir extent vs. dam point locations.
globalSurfaceWater.limitations: 30m resolution means small streams and ponds below ~900m² are invisible. Cloud-persistent regions (tropical rainforests) have lower observation counts and less reliable seasonal classification. The 2021 endpoint means very recent changes (new dams, droughts) may not yet be reflected. Ice and snow can be misclassified as water in polar and high-altitude regions.

treeCoverLoss.label: Tree Cover Loss
treeCoverLoss.source: University of Maryland / WRI — umd_tree_cover_loss v1.13, tiles.globalforestwatch.org. Hansen et al. 2013.
treeCoverLoss.updateFreq: Annual, following UMD's own release cadence
treeCoverLoss.description: Annual deforestation at 30 m resolution. Detects complete canopy removal from any cause: logging, agriculture, fire, mining or urbanisation.
treeCoverLoss.reading: Each pixel carries the year its tree cover was lost, so deforestation near a mine can be read as a sequence rather than a single state.

forestCarbonFlux.label: Forest Carbon Flux
forestCarbonFlux.source: WRI / Global Forest Watch — gfw_forest_carbon_net_flux v20250430, tiles.globalforestwatch.org. Harris et al. 2021 and Gibbs et al. 2025.
forestCarbonFlux.updateFreq: Annual, following Global Forest Watch's own release cadence
forestCarbonFlux.description: Net CO₂ emissions and removals per hectare at 30 m resolution, 2001–2025. Quantifies the carbon consequences of deforestation — how much CO₂ is released when a forest is cleared for mining, and how much is taken back up by regrowth on abandoned sites.
forestCarbonFlux.reading: Red pixels are net emissions (deforestation), green pixels net sequestration (regrowth). Cross-reference with Mining Footprints to weigh the carbon cost of land clearing for extraction.

soilOrganicCarbon.label: Soil Organic Carbon
soilOrganicCarbon.updateFreq: Static — served from ISRIC's SoilGrids WMS at maps.isric.org, refreshed when ISRIC issues a new release
soilOrganicCarbon.description: Global soil organic carbon, top 0–5 cm at ~250 m resolution. Soil organic carbon is the largest terrestrial carbon pool. Mining operations strip topsoil and destroy this carbon store permanently. This layer, when active, will show how much soil carbon is at risk in mining areas.
soilOrganicCarbon.reading: Darker means higher carbon density (tonnes C/ha). Cross-reference with Mining Footprints to see how much soil carbon sits inside an area already stripped.

waterRisk.label: Water Risk (Aqueduct)
waterRisk.source: WRI Aqueduct 4.0 — Kuzma et al. 2023. CC BY 4.0. 68,506 sub-basin polygons globally.
waterRisk.description: Global water risk scored at sub-basin level using 13 indicators: water stress, depletion, variability, drought risk, flood risk, and regulatory/reputational risk. Each polygon is the intersection of a HydroBASIN Level 6 sub-basin, an administrative province, and a groundwater aquifer. Scores use the mining industry weighting scheme — tuned to the water challenges most relevant to mining operations.
waterRisk.reading: Polygons colored by mining-weighted overall water risk: pale yellow = Low, gold = Low-Medium, orange = Medium-High, red = High, dark red = Extremely High, neutral grey = No data. Click any polygon to see individual indicator scores (water stress, depletion, drought, flood). Overlay with Mining Footprints or Tailings Dams to identify facilities in water-stressed basins — a key factor in dam failure risk and community water conflicts.
waterRisk.colorStandard: WRI Aqueduct 4.0 official 5-class palette (wri.org/aqueduct). 'No data' uses neutral grey, never a risk color.
