offshoreActivities.updateFreq: Synced weekly from authoritative government registries; syncs run 45 min after service boot then weekly
offshoreActivities.description: Government-issued concessions for offshore oil and gas production, offshore wind farms, seabed mining, and carbon capture & storage (CCS) inside national Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and Extended Continental Shelf (ECS) jurisdictions. Covers ~70% of global EEZ exploitation. ISA's 'The Area' (international waters beyond EEZ) is covered by the Mining Concessions layer, not this one.
offshoreActivities.reading: Amber/red = oil and gas concession; sky blue = offshore wind lease; magenta = seabed mining licence; emerald = CCS (carbon capture & storage) licence. Click any block for operator name, sovereign country, status, lease dates, and a direct link to the authoritative government registry. Use the activity-type chips to show only one type, and the Country chips, to narrow to a specific sovereign (US 2,065 · UK 1,115 · Norway 1,080 · Brazil 276 · Canada 193 · Denmark 98 · …). The North Sea and US Gulf are the densest regions to explore first.
offshoreActivities.limitations: ~70% global coverage. Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, Qatar/UAE, Nigeria, Angola, and most of sub-Saharan Africa are PDF-only registries not yet machine-readable. NZP&M and MRA PNG REST endpoints are provisional and may go offline. ANP Brazil uses an ArcGIS hosted service — the official monthly SHP downloads are more complete but require manual extraction. The GEUS Denmark WFS is pinned to the 4326.jsp path (CRS84); the sister 25832.jsp path returns UTM Zone 32N meters and was fixed after initial ingestion stored features at lat ≈ 6,000,000. C-NLOPB exploration parcels in the Grand Banks / Flemish Pass area (22 of 105 features) sit on Canada's Extended Continental Shelf beyond the 200-nm EEZ and won't appear under the Canada country filter. ECS jurisdiction is otherwise simplified to EEZ for sovereign tagging.

hydrophone-stations.label: Hydrophone Stations
hydrophone-stations.description: Passive acoustic monitoring stations from twenty-three official observatory and research networks: Ocean Observatories Initiative (US Pacific NW), Integrated Marine Observing System (Australia), MBARI MARS (Monterey Bay), AWI PALAOA (Antarctic Ocean), AWI HAUSGARTEN / FRAM Observatory (7 moored hydrophones in the Fram Strait, CC BY 4.0, via PANGAEA), SAMBAH — Static Acoustic Monitoring of the Baltic Sea Harbour Porpoise (~298 C-POD stations across all Baltic nations, 2011–2013, CC0 1.0, via Dryad), CTBTO IMS — International Monitoring System hydroacoustic network (11 global stations, treaty-disclosed positions, structurally static, CTBTO Preparatory Commission), OBSEA (Spanish Mediterranean shelf), KM3NeT (deep Mediterranean neutrino telescope sites), plus the full NOAA Passive Acoustic Archive — NRS (global reference stations), SanctSound (US National Marine Sanctuaries), NEFSC (Northeast Fisheries Science Center, including the Stellwagen Bank Cornell MARU array), PIFSC (Pacific Islands HARPs), SEFSC (Gulf of Mexico HARPs), ONMS (newer sanctuary uploads), ADEON (Atlantic Deepwater Ecosystem Observation Network), BOEM (offshore wind PAM, Atlantic and Gulf), AEON (Atlantic Ecosystem Observation Network), US Navy (MBARC LMR + USWTR), National Park Service (Glacier Bay), JASCO (ESRF Atlantic Canada), FRAM (Alfred Wegener Institute, Fram Strait Arctic), Coastal Studies Institute (NCROEP, Hatteras), and IOOS ESONS (estuarine soundscape). Phase 1 surfaces station metadata only — soundscape SPL products require Phase 3 work to compute from NetCDF source audio.
hydrophone-stations.reading: Click a station to see its hardware, depth, deployment window, and a link to raw audio recordings at the operator's portal. When Phase 3 ships, the sparkline area will populate with broadband SPL trend and ISO 18405 third-octave band breakdown (10 Hz / 63 Hz / 100 Hz / 125 Hz / 1 kHz / 10 kHz) plus L50/L95 percentile statistics.
hydrophone-stations.limitations: Phase 1 does not display numeric soundscape data — none of the twenty-three networks publishes pre-aggregated daily SPL products via a public REST API. Raw recordings are available via the portal link (and via NOAA's public Google Cloud Storage bucket noaa-passive-bioacoustic for the fifteen NOAA-archive programs). ONC hydrophones in BC Pacific are on a separate layer. PALAOA was decommissioned ~late 2017 after Neumayer III cable damage. NEFSC Stellwagen Bank MARUs are historic 2007-2010; ADEON 2017-2019; AEON 2022-2024; Navy MBARC 2006-2014; Navy USWTR 2007-2008; NPS Glacier Bay 2011-present (cabled). SAMBAH C-POD data are a completed 2011–2013 project (historic). SWFSC drifter / glider deployments and AFSC sonobuoy records are excluded because they have no static position to render on the map.

bathymetry.label: Seafloor Bathymetry
bathymetry.source: GEBCO Compilation Group · GEBCO_2026 Grid via wms.gebco.net (public, CC0)
bathymetry.updateFreq: GEBCO releases a new grid annually in mid-year
bathymetry.description: Shaded-relief depth map of the entire ocean floor — 15 arc-second resolution global bathymetry from GEBCO (General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans), the canonical IHO/IOC product. Free, no attribution gate beyond the chip in the panel. Provides physical context for every other sea layer: which Argo floats sit over abyssal plain vs. seamount, which ISA concessions overlap mid-ocean ridges, which vents cluster on plate boundaries.
bathymetry.reading: Lighter shading = shallower seafloor. Darker shading = deeper. Steep grey-to-light transitions trace seamounts, ridges, trenches and continental shelves. Layer is off by default — toggle on to add seafloor context to whatever else you're viewing.
bathymetry.limitations: Roughly 25% of the ocean floor has been directly surveyed (Seabed 2030 target). The remainder is interpolated from satellite-altimetry gravity inversions and adjacent ship tracks. Real seafloor resolution at any given point can be much coarser than the 15 arc-sec grid suggests, especially in remote ocean basins.

woa-climatology.label: Ocean Climatology (WOA)
woa-climatology.source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information — World Ocean Atlas 2023 (WOA23). ncei.noaa.gov/data/oceans/woa/WOA23/DATA/ · NCEI Accession 0270533
woa-climatology.description: Objectively-analysed gridded ocean climatology from the World Ocean Atlas 2023. A colour-field raster is overlaid on the globe for the chosen variable and depth. At 0 m / 50 m you can see warm surface water pooling in the tropics, cold subpolar gyres, and equatorial upwelling tongues. At 500–1000 m the oxygen-minimum zones (OMZs) appear as dark swaths across the eastern Pacific and Arabian Sea — exactly the depths targeted by nodule mining. Nutrient-rich upwelling systems and warm-core rings stand out in the dissolved nutrients fields.
woa-climatology.reading: Colour encodes the magnitude of the selected variable at the chosen depth. Use the Variable selector to switch between dissolved oxygen (µmol/kg), temperature (°C), salinity (PSS-78), apparent oxygen utilisation, percent O₂ saturation, phosphate, silicate, and nitrate. Use the Depth selector to step through the eight standard levels (0, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 m). The colour scale (CMAP) is variable-specific and defined in the WOA23 product — see NCEI for the per-variable legend.
woa-climatology.limitations: 1° horizontal resolution; annual mean climatology only — seasonal cycle and interannual variability are not shown. Baseline periods differ by variable: temperature and salinity use 1991–2020, dissolved oxygen / AOU / percent saturation use 1971–2000, and phosphate / silicate / nitrate use 1965–2022. Sparse in-situ observations in the Southern Ocean and Arctic may reduce reliability at depth. The PNG colour-field is a pre-baked RGBA texture; numeric values are not available via click.

oxygen-deox.label: Ocean Oxygen & Deoxygenation
oxygen-deox.description: Recent dissolved oxygen from ISAS BGC-Argo floats (2014–2018), plus a change (Δ) view comparing it to the WOA23 1971–2000 “Climate Normal” baseline.
oxygen-deox.reading: Recent view: blue = high O₂, red = low (oxygen minimum zones). Δ view: red = oxygen loss since 1971–2000, blue = gain.
oxygen-deox.limitations: Indicative regional pattern of oxygen change, not a calibrated trend. The recent field (Argo optodes, 2014–2018) and the 1971–2000 baseline (ship Winkler/CTD) differ in instrument and method, so some apparent change reflects that difference. Clicking the map returns the recent value, the baseline and their difference for the nearest grid cell; the coloured field behind them is a pre-baked image, so a click samples that cell, not the exact pixel.
oxygen-deox.source: ISAS20 BGC-Argo O₂ — Kolodziejczyk, Prigent-Mazella & Gaillard 2023, SEANOE 10.17882/52367 (CC-BY 4.0); method: Kolodziejczyk et al. 2024, ESSD 16:5191; baseline WOA23, NOAA NCEI.

arctic-rivers.label: Arctic River Inputs
arctic-rivers.description: Discharge and biogeochemistry at the mouths of the great Arctic rivers — the land-to-ocean transfer of freshwater, carbon, and nutrients into the Arctic Ocean. Two sub-sources, each independently toggleable: ArcticGRO (Arctic Great Rivers Observatory) monitors the 6 largest Arctic rivers (Ob', Yenisey, Lena, Kolyma, Yukon, Mackenzie) — dissolved organic carbon, nutrients, major ions and the river discharge measured on each sampling date, sampled ~6 times per year since ~2003; PANGAEA dataset PANGAEA.945702 (Brown et al. 2022) adds Canadian Arctic Archipelago rivers (DOC, nutrients, water isotopes). Together these capture the dominant observed biogeochemical inputs to the Arctic Ocean — a critical boundary condition for how permafrost thaw and land-use change reach the sea.
arctic-rivers.reading: Each dot is a river monitoring station, coloured by data source (ArcticGRO / PANGAEA Canada). Click for the period of record and the observed time series: dissolved organic carbon and nutrient concentrations, plus river discharge at each sampling date for ArcticGRO rivers. For Canadian Arctic (PANGAEA) stations, water isotopes (δ¹⁸O, δD) and — where measured — water temperature and conductivity are shown under Water Properties. Values are the contributors' published measurements; series are shown at monthly resolution.
arctic-rivers.limitations: Methods are heterogeneous across sources and eras (sampling frequency, lab protocols). Biogeochemistry and discharge are sampled only ~6 times per year at ArcticGRO stations, which can miss episodic events (ice-melt pulses, storm runoff); monthly display further smooths this. Discharge shown is the value on the sampling date, not a continuous daily series — so true annual discharge volumes and integrated carbon/nutrient export loads are not computed in this version (a planned enhancement using the full daily-discharge records). PANGAEA.913197 (Lena/Samoylov high-frequency biogeochem) is a PANGAEA collection without a single machine-readable file and is not yet ingested. ArcticGRO covers only the 6 largest rivers; hundreds of smaller Arctic rivers are not represented.
arctic-rivers.source: ArcticGRO — Arctic Great Rivers Observatory (arcticgreatrivers.org/data), free to use, credit ArcticGRO; PANGAEA dataset PANGAEA.945702 (Brown et al. 2022, Canadian Arctic Archipelago rivers), CC-BY-4.0.
arctic-rivers.updateFreq: ArcticGRO periodic data releases; PANGAEA dataset static (DOI-versioned)

wod-oxygen.label: Historical Oxygen Profiles (WOD)
wod-oxygen.description: Raw dissolved-oxygen vertical profiles from NOAA World Ocean Database 2023, global coverage. Each dot is one oceanographic cast — a ship station or profiling float that lowered a sensor to depth and measured O₂ at multiple levels. Dots are coloured by the decade the cast was collected, letting you see how sampling coverage has changed from the 1900s to the 2020s. At wide zoom the dots are thinned to a representative sample for performance; zoom in for full detail.
wod-oxygen.reading: dots = individual O₂ casts, colour = decade; click for the full depth–O₂ profile
wod-oxygen.limitations: "Deepest sample" is how deep the cast went, not how deep the sea is — it is the deepest level with a valid O₂ reading. Do not filter on it to isolate the continental shelf: 480,822 of the 978,476 casts sampled no deeper than 150 m, and they lie everywhere from 78° S to 89° N, including open-ocean surface casts. Filtering that way returns surface-saturation values and makes every known dead zone look healthy. True seafloor depth is shown separately in the click panel, sampled from GEBCO. Raw heterogeneous methods and QC: early casts (pre-1960s) used Winkler titration; later casts use electrochemical or optode sensors. QC flags are those published by NOAA NCEI — they have not been re-evaluated here. Coverage reflects the historical distribution of ship expeditions — dense in the North Atlantic and North Pacific, sparse in the Southern Ocean and early decades. Units are as published (typically µmol kg⁻¹ or ml l⁻¹); no unit conversion is applied.

memento.label: MEMENTO (Marine CH₄/N₂O)
memento.description: Research cruise casts of dissolved methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) from the GEOMAR MEMENTO portal — a frozen community archive of ~12,000 surface and near-surface measurements collected between the 1980s and ~2020. Each dot is one cruise cast; colour indicates CH₄ or N₂O surface concentration relative to cruise-biased global coverage.
memento.reading: dots = individual casts, colour = selected gas surface concentration (teal low → magenta high); click for the full depth profile and sample table; switch to Hexagons for density overview
memento.limitations: Values coded -999 are no-data sentinels, not measurements. Quality flags are stored in the params object (WOCE conventions: 2=good, 4=suspect; 9=missing, stored as 0.00). MEMENTO publishes dissolved and atmospheric gas under one column name — CH₄ is both Methane_Ocean [nmol/l] and Methane_Atmosphere [ppb] — and the CSV export omits the distinction. Where a contributor did not label a sample _Air, this platform inferred which values are atmospheric from the cruise median and marks them “air”; that inference is ours, not MEMENTO's. No value is modified or removed — flagged values remain in the panel and in Area Export. Coverage is cruise-biased: dense in the North Atlantic and North Sea, sparse in the South Pacific and Southern Ocean. Some cruises submitted unpublished data — if you plan to publish, you must contact the contributing scientist for permission.
memento.sources: GEOMAR MEMENTO — memento.geomar.de (data portal: portal.geomar.de/memento). Database citation required by MEMENTO's terms of use: Kock, A. and Bange, H. W. (2015) Counting the ocean's greenhouse gas emissions, Eos 96(3), 10-13, doi:10.1029/2015EO023665. Their terms also require this acknowledgement: “The MEMENTO database is administered by the Kiel Data Management Team at GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research and supported by the German BMBF project SOPRAN (Surface Ocean Processes in the Anthropocene, http://sopran.pangaea.de). The database is accessible through the MEMENTO webpage: https://memento.geomar.de.” Cite the original publications too if you use fewer than 10 individual data submissions. Project paper: Bange et al. (2009) MEMENTO: a proposal to develop a database of marine nitrous oxide and methane measurements, Environ. Chem. doi:10.1071/en09033.

methane-seeps.label: Methane Seeps (SEAFLEA)
methane-seeps.description: Global inventory of known seafloor methane seep sites from the SEAFLEA Observed Database, compiled by Phrampus et al. (2020) from NRL (Naval Research Laboratory) and NOAA NCEI archival sources. Each dot represents a confirmed seep location with one or more classified feature types — gas bubbles/flares, gas hydrates, mounds, pockmarks, chemosynthetic communities, or carbonate hardgrounds. It is a compilation of published seep studies, not a systematic global survey — coverage follows survey effort, not seep abundance. ~10,386 seep records globally.
methane-seeps.reading: dots = individual seep sites, colour = primary feature type (red = gas bubbles, cyan = hydrate, amber = mound, blue = pockmark, green = chemosynthetic community, purple = carbonate hardground, slate = unclassified); click for all confirmed feature types, depth, year observed, and source reference; use the feature-type chevron filter to focus on a single type
methane-seeps.limitations: Coverage is survey-biased, and this is the layer's most important caveat. The 10,385 records come from just 32 published studies, and one BOEM seismic survey of the Gulf of Mexico supplies 6,126 of them (59%). Whole regions are blank because nobody has looked: there are zero mapped seeps in the central North Sea, and the nearest seep to it lies 418 km away. An absent dot means an absent survey, not an absent seep — never read this layer as evidence that a region has no natural methane source. Frozen Feb-2019 compilation — seep discoveries reported after that date are not included. 72% of records have no reported observation year (depth and year fields shown as '—' or 'not recorded'); depth is stored as a text field in the source. Location uncertainty can reach several km for acoustically detected seeps. A single seep site may carry multiple feature type flags (multi-flag entries) — click to see all flags; the primary type (highest-priority flag) drives the map colour. Uncertain identifications flagged U(…) in the source are retained and labeled accordingly.
methane-seeps.source: Phrampus, B.J. et al. (2020). A Global Probabilistic Prediction of Cold Seeps and Associated SEAfloor FLuid Expulsion Anomalies (SEAFLEAs). Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems, 21. doi:10.1029/2019GC008747. Archived at NOAA NCEI / NRL SEAFLEA dataset, ArcGIS FeatureServer layer 6.

geotraces.label: Trace Metals (GEOTRACES)
geotraces.description: Water-column vertical profiles of dissolved trace metals — manganese (Mn), iron (Fe), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni), and copper (Cu) — from the GEOTRACES Intermediate Data Product 2025 (IDP2025). These five elements are the primary metals concentrated in seafloor polymetallic nodules and cobalt-rich crusts, the targets of deep-sea mining. GEOTRACES is an international programme coordinating high-precision trace-element and isotope measurements across global ocean transects; IDP2025 covers ~2003–2023.
geotraces.reading: Select an element using the layer controls. Each dot on the map is a GEOTRACES sampling station, coloured by its peak (maximum) concentration measured anywhere in the water column. Click a station for the full concentration-vs-depth profile. Near-bottom enrichment — a spike in the profile at the deepest levels — is the signal most relevant to deep-sea mining: it can indicate mobilisation of metals from disturbed seafloor sediments or resuspended nodule material. Units differ by element: Co is measured in pmol/kg; Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu in nmol/kg. SeaDataNet quality flags are shown in the profile; values flagged as below detection limit are labelled accordingly.
geotraces.limitations: Research-grade dataset, not continuous environmental monitoring. Spatial coverage is sparse and transect-biased — dense across Atlantic, Pacific, and Southern Ocean sections but absent from many coastal and marginal seas. IDP2025 is a static archive (no live updates); some metals, particularly Co, are more sparsely sampled than Fe or Mn. Quality flags follow SeaDataNet conventions (1 = good, 2 = probably good, 4 = bad, 9 = missing). The mining-relevance interpretation (near-bottom enrichment) is contextual — enrichment also occurs naturally near hydrothermal vents and oxygen-minimum zones.
geotraces.sources: GEOTRACES Intermediate Data Product 2025 (IDP2025), NERC EDS British Oceanographic Data Centre (BODC). doi:10.5285/42c92148-8d03-8be6-e063-7086abc09f0c. Licence: CC-BY 4.0.

ocean-carbon.label: Ocean Carbon (GLODAP)
ocean-carbon.source: Key, R.M. et al. (2015) Global Ocean Data Analysis Project Version 2 (GLODAPv2) — Mapped product. CDIAC, https://doi.org/10.3334/CDIAC/OTG.NDP093_GLODAPv2 · glodap.info/index.php/mapped-data-product/
ocean-carbon.description: Global climatology of the ocean carbon system based on quality-controlled ship-board measurements compiled by the GLODAP consortium. Four variables are mapped on a 1° grid at 33 depth levels using DIVA (Data-Interpolating Variational Analysis): dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), total alkalinity (TAlk), pH, and anthropogenic CO₂ (Cant). These are the fundamental quantities that determine ocean acidification and the ocean's capacity to absorb atmospheric CO₂ — including in the deep waters targeted by seabed mining.
ocean-carbon.reading: Colour encodes the magnitude of the selected variable at the chosen depth. Use the Variable selector to switch between DIC (µmol/kg), Total Alkalinity (µmol/kg), pH, and anthropogenic CO₂ Cant (µmol/kg). Use the Depth selector to step through levels from 0 to 4000 m. Exact numeric values are only available in the hexagon view — switch to Hexagons and click a cell.
ocean-carbon.limitations: 1° horizontal resolution; gap-filled DIVA interpolation smooths fine-scale gradients and introduces artefacts in data-sparse regions (Southern Ocean, Arctic). Mapped product frozen at GLODAPv2.2016b — does not reflect post-2016 observations or the accelerating acidification trend of the past decade. The PNG colour-field is a pre-baked RGBA texture; numeric values are not available via click in the field view.

ocean-co2-surface.label: Surface Ocean CO₂ (SOCAT)
ocean-co2-surface.source: Bakker, D.C.E. et al. / SOCAT community (2025) Surface Ocean CO₂ Atlas (SOCAT) version 2026. NCEI Accession 0315110, https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/ocean-carbon-acidification-data-system-portal/ · socat.info
ocean-co2-surface.description: Decadal 1° climatological grid of surface-ocean CO₂ fugacity (fCO₂) derived from the SOCATv2026 quality-controlled ship-track database. Four mapped variables per decade: fugacity of CO₂ (fCO₂, µatm), observation density (number of 1-minute bins), sea-surface temperature (SST, °C), and salinity (psu). Covers the 1970s through 2020s. Source observations come from research vessels, merchant ships, and autonomous sensors worldwide — the largest public collection of surface-ocean CO₂ measurements.
ocean-co2-surface.reading: Variable selector fCO₂ / observation density / SST / salinity; decade selector 1970s–2020s; colour field shows the global distribution for the chosen variable and decade. Exact numeric values are only available in the hexagon view — switch to Hexagons and click a cell.
ocean-co2-surface.limitations: Non-gap-filled product — approximately 21% of 1° cells have data, concentrated along ship tracks; large regions of the Southern Ocean, Arctic, and coastal seas have no coverage in early decades. Pre-baked RGBA texture in field view — exact values only in hexagon view. Static SOCATv2026 release — does not include cruises submitted after the 2026 data cutoff.

marine-carbon.label: Marine Carbon (unified)
marine-carbon.source: Co-located readout combining GLODAP v2.2016b (DIC/TAlk/pH/Cant), SOCAT v2026 (surface fCO₂), ISAS20 (oxygen) and WOA23 (temperature/salinity/nutrients). glodap.info · socat.info · ncei.noaa.gov/products/world-ocean-atlas
marine-carbon.description: One hexagon grid that brings together every carbon-related ocean field at a single location. Click any cell to read surface CO₂ (SOCAT), interior carbon — DIC, total alkalinity, pH, anthropogenic CO₂ (GLODAP), dissolved oxygen and its change versus the historical baseline (ISAS/WOA), and physical climatology — temperature, salinity, nutrients (WOA) — side by side, each labelled with its own source and units. Designed so you can read the land-to-ocean carbon picture at one spot without toggling six separate layers.
marine-carbon.reading: Colour encodes the variable picked in the Variable selector (surface fCO₂, interior DIC, dissolved O₂, or temperature) at the chosen depth. Click a cell to open the full readout: every source's value at that location, grouped by source, with 'no data here' shown where a source does not cover the cell. Surface CO₂ is always sampled at the surface (latest decade) regardless of the selected depth, because it is an air–sea exchange quantity.
marine-carbon.limitations: A co-located readout, NOT a fused metric — the values come from four independent climatologies at different native resolutions, periods and depths and must not be combined into one number. GLODAP and WOA are 1° gap-filled climatologies that smooth fine-scale gradients; SOCAT surface CO₂ is sparse (~21% of cells, mostly ship tracks); ISAS oxygen reflects a 2014–2018 mean. All four are static releases and do not reflect the most recent years.

vme-suitability.label: VME Suitability (modeled)
vme-suitability.source: NOAA Deep-Sea Coral & Sponge (DSCRTP) occurrences of reef-forming stony corals, modeled against GEBCO 2024 (bathymetry/slope), seabed substrate (Dutkiewicz et al. 2015), WOA23 (temperature/salinity/nutrients), ISAS20 (oxygen) and GLODAPv2.2016b (carbon chemistry) predictors using a MaxEnt species-distribution model (elapid). services2.arcgis.com/C8EMgrsFcRFL6LrL/arcgis/rest/services/DSCRTP_NatDB
vme-suitability.description: Modeled habitat suitability for two reef-forming deep-sea coral species, Desmophyllum pertusum (formerly Lophelia pertusa) and Solenosmilia variabilis, on the hexagon grid. The model learns the environmental conditions at known coral occurrences and scores every cell by how similar its environment is, using predictors sampled at the seafloor depth of each cell.
vme-suitability.reading: The Suitability view colours each hexagon 0 (least similar) to 1 (most similar to known VME habitat) — this is a relative similarity score, not a probability of presence. The Uncertainty view shows the spread across a cross-validation ensemble of model runs at the same cell; higher spread means the model is less confident, typically in poorly sampled or environmentally unusual areas. Colours run dark purple (low) → blue → teal → green → yellow (high). The Uncertainty view reuses the same ramp, rescaled to its own range: dark = low spread (more confident), yellow = high spread (less confident).
vme-suitability.limitations: This is a MODELED layer, not observed data — no dot on this layer means a coral was seen there. The score is a relative environmental-similarity index, NOT a probability of species presence and NOT evidence that a vulnerable marine ecosystem exists at that location. Training occurrences come from DSCRTP survey effort, which is geographically uneven (concentrated where surveys have happened, e.g. US and NE Atlantic waters) — the model can only be as good as where it has been shown examples. The model uses a target-group background (other DSCRTP coral/sponge records as pseudo-absences), which does not fully correct for that sampling bias. Predictions in environments far outside the sampled range (e.g. unusually shallow, warm, or low-oxygen combinations) are extrapolations and are less reliable — the Uncertainty view is the best guide to where that applies. Predictors are sampled at the seafloor depth per cell as an approximation, not a true 3-D water-column match. This layer must not be used for causal or impact inference — it describes environmental similarity to known habitat, not measured ecological impact.
vme-suitability.method:
How this layer is built — a MaxEnt species-distribution model (SDM), not observed data.

Response data: occurrence records of two reef-forming stony corals — Desmophyllum pertusum (formerly Lophelia pertusa) and Solenosmilia variabilis — from NOAA's Deep-Sea Coral & Sponge database (DSCRTP), resolved to WoRMS AphiaIDs and spatially thinned to one record per hexagon per species to reduce sampling clustering (167 usable presences in the current bake).

Background: presence-only data has no true absences, so the model draws 'target-group background' points from all DSCRTP coral survey locations — correcting for where sampling effort actually went, rather than treating unsurveyed ocean as unsuitable.

Predictors (6), each sampled at the seafloor (matched to the GEBCO seafloor depth beneath each point, never the surface): seafloor depth & terrain (GEBCO 2024); temperature & salinity (WOA23); dissolved oxygen (ISAS20); seabed substrate (Dutkiewicz et al. 2015); and aragonite saturation state Ω, derived from GLODAPv2.2016b dissolved inorganic carbon + total alkalinity via the PyCO2SYS carbonate-system solver (calcifying corals track Ω).

Model & evaluation: a MaxEnt model (elapid) is fit with spatial-block cross-validation (ordinary random CV inflates skill on clustered occurrences). The per-fold models form an ensemble — the mean prediction is the suitability score, the spread across folds is the uncertainty. Skill is reported as AUC and the continuous Boyce index; a species is published only if AUC ≥ 0.70, Boyce > 0 and ≥ 50 thinned occurrences. The current model scores AUC 0.89 / Boyce 0.51.

Reading the output: suitability is a RELATIVE score from 0 to 1 — how environmentally similar a cell is to known VME habitat — not a probability that corals are present, and not evidence that they are. The Uncertainty view shows the cross-validation ensemble spread; cells whose predictors fall outside the sampled range are flagged as extrapolated.

Limitations: coverage is limited to cells where every predictor exists at the seafloor (~3,800 hexagons in the current bake); occurrence data carry survey-effort bias; seafloor depth-matching is an approximation; and this layer must never be used for causal or impact inference.

colorRamp.label: 1.00 — most suitable (closest to known VME habitat)

sios-svalbard.label: SIOS Svalbard Observing
sios-svalbard.description: Dataset-discovery layer for in-situ observing datasets in and around Svalbard, harvested from the SIOS (Svalbard Integrated Arctic Earth Observing System) Station REST catalogue. Each point is a dataset; in the By-station view, an observing platform. Each links out to the underlying data (OPeNDAP / HTTP / WMS). Coverage is currently centred on the Polish Polar Station Hornsund (Institute of Geophysics, Polish Academy of Sciences) Core Data series and expands automatically as SIOS adds platform metadata for more stations.
sios-svalbard.reading: dots = individual observing stations/platforms; colour by dataset category (single colour here — use the three-view filter to switch between Core Data, All datasets, and By station); click for station name, institution, principal investigator, activity type, time coverage, variables, abstract, and direct links to OPeNDAP, HTTP download, WMS map service, and the dataset landing page; links are served live from the SIOS METSIS catalogue
sios-svalbard.limitations: Discovery / metadata layer only — the measurements are served by the originating institution via the links in the click panel. Coverage is small and currently dominated by the Hornsund (IGF PAS) Core Data (~25 datasets): only datasets exposed with in-situ platform metadata in the SIOS Station REST appear here. Most of the wider SIOS / METSIS catalogue is satellite or modelled data that merely covers Svalbard rather than in-situ Svalbard observations, and is out of scope. Point positions are the centroid of the dataset's reported bounding box (not a GPS fix), so area datasets may be off by a few km.
sios-svalbard.source: SIOS METSIS catalogue REST endpoint: sios-svalbard.org/rest/stations/data.json · Browse at: sios-svalbard.org/metsis/search · Per-dataset licences: CC-BY or CC-BY-SA (stated on each landing page)

arctic-catchments.label: Arctic Catchments (ARCADE)
arctic-catchments.description: Pan-Arctic catchment polygons from ARCADE v1 (Arctic Catchment database for River Discharge and Ecology), each attributed with modelled soil organic carbon stock, total organic carbon, runoff, permafrost extent, and ERA5-Land-derived mean air temperature. These catchments are the terrestrial source areas that feed the rivers monitored by the Arctic River Inputs layer, making them the key link in land–ocean carbon and water coupling in the Arctic system.
arctic-catchments.reading: The variable selector recolours the choropleth by the chosen attribute (soil carbon, runoff, permafrost extent, or mean air temperature in °C). Click a catchment polygon to open the full attribute profile in the click panel. Polygons were originally defined on the EASE-Grid 2.0 equal-area projection and have been reprojected to WGS 84 for display.
arctic-catchments.limitations: Catchment boundaries are reprojected from EASE-Grid 2.0; centroids and edges carry ~km-level positional uncertainty from the grid-cell to polygon conversion. Climate values (temperature, runoff) are ERA5-Land reanalysis-derived long-term means, not in-situ measurements. Organic carbon values are modelled soil stock estimates from SoilGrids-based sources, not measured flux data. Runoff is in source units (approximately 0–2.8) and the exact physical unit (mm/yr or equivalent) is not asserted. Some catchments have no name. This is a static archive (ARCADE v1 release). Catchments crossing the antimeridian (~10 small Bering Strait basins) are omitted — polar-projection wrapping distorts their geometry.
arctic-catchments.source: ARCADE v1 — Arctic Catchment database for River Discharge and Ecology. DataVerse NL. doi:10.34894/U9HSPV. Licence: CC-BY 4.0.

area-export.label: Area Export
area-export.description: Download tool — select an area of interest (bounding box, polygon, or hex-cell set) and download raw data records from one or more layers as GeoJSON or CSV. The Export panel groups ~30 layers into seven families: ISA & seabed, Life & geology, Sensors, Infrastructure, Carbon fields, Land, and Arctic & carbon. Tick any combination across families, choose GeoJSON or CSV with the format toggle, then click ↓ Download selected (ZIP) to receive a single ZIP archive — one file per selected layer. Composite layers expand to sub-folders: marine-carbon produces four files (GLODAP DIC/TAlk/pH/Cant, SOCAT fCO₂, ISAS O₂, WOA climatology); submarine-cables produces one file per sub-source (EMODnet, NOAA, NZ LINZ, AU ACMA, ONC, OOI). A MANIFEST.txt at the archive root lists every included file with its layer id, upstream source name, and record count. Each file carries provenance metadata (source name, source URL, citation, licence) so results can be verified against the original upstream dataset. Values are verbatim upstream values — the platform does not alter or derive them. An API key is required.
area-export.reading: Open the Export panel (footer → Export), use the toolbar to draw an area, tick one or more layers from the grouped checklist, pick GeoJSON or CSV with the format toggle, then click ↓ Download selected (ZIP). Keys are issued to approved organisations via the org portal at apiv2.something-rare.com/org-ui/. Use the /v2/export/{layer}/count endpoint to preview record counts before downloading. The bundle endpoint /v2/export/bundle accepts a comma-separated layers= list plus the same bbox/polygon/cell_ids parameters as single-layer exports.
area-export.limitations: Each layer has a hard per-request cap (visible as '⚠ capped at N' next to the count); there is no paging — if your area of interest is too large, reduce it or check the count endpoint first. The hex-select mode only draws from monitoring-density hex cells that already hold data; it cannot select arbitrary ocean areas (use bounding-box or polygon for that). Derived/rollup layers (monitoring density grid, unified marine-carbon hex colours, WOA hex grids) are ineligible — only the rawest underlying tables are exported. Client-side-only layers (ports, tectonic plates) have no Postgres table and are not exportable. API keys are granted to approved organisations only; there is no public self-signup.
area-export.source: Data provenance varies by layer — each download carries 'source', 'source_url', and 'citation' fields. Verify individual records at the upstream source listed in those fields. Bundle API: apiv2.something-rare.com/v2/export/bundle · Single-layer API: apiv2.something-rare.com/v2/export/{layer}

seabed-substrate.label: Seabed Substrate
seabed-substrate.description: Global map of seafloor sediment type — 13 lithology classes interpolated by a support-vector-machine from descriptions of ~14,500 seafloor samples, at 0.1° resolution.
seabed-substrate.reading: Colour = dominant lithology class. Field mode shows the full-resolution choropleth; Hexagons mode is clickable and reports the class at each cell. Clay dominates the abyssal plains (nodule terrain); calcareous oozes sit above the carbonate compensation depth.
seabed-substrate.limitations: A model, not a per-site assay: 0.1° resolution smooths local variation and class boundaries are interpolated. License is CC-BY-NC (non-commercial).

arctic-sediment-carbon.label: Arctic Sediment Carbon
arctic-sediment-carbon.source: CASCADE v2 — Martens et al. 2021, ESSD 13:2561; Bolin Centre Database (bolin.su.se/data/cascade)
arctic-sediment-carbon.description: Organic carbon in Arctic Ocean surface sediments from the Circum-Arctic Sediment Carbon Database. Field view: interpolated 5 km rasters of OC, TN, δ¹³C, Δ¹⁴C. Stations view: ~4,500 raw sampling stations.
arctic-sediment-carbon.reading: Higher organic carbon and more negative δ¹³C/Δ¹⁴C indicate terrestrial (land-derived) carbon deposited on the seafloor — the sink of carbon exported by Arctic rivers and eroding permafrost coasts.
arctic-sediment-carbon.limitations: Field view is interpolated (modelled), not measured. Surface sediments only (0–5 cm). Not every station has every parameter. CC-BY 4.0.

permafrost-thaw.label: Permafrost Thaw
permafrost-thaw.description: 19,540 observed permafrost thaw feature locations across Alaska (Webb et al. 2026, ESSD) — thermokarst lakes, retrogressive thaw slumps, active-layer detachments, thermokarst wetlands, thermo-erosional gullies, wildfire-induced thaw and thaw ponds — plus ~40,102 circumpolar retrogressive thaw slump points from the ARTS inventory (whrc/ARTS v6.0.0, Yang, Rodenhizer, Rogers et al. 2025, Sci. Data 12:18, CC0), spanning Siberia, Canada and the wider Eurasian Arctic. The terrestrial abrupt-thaw signal that mobilises carbon into Arctic rivers and coasts.
permafrost-thaw.reading: Each dot is one observed thaw feature, coloured by category. Click for the source publication (with DOI), observation method (field vs remote sensing), and imagery used. Filter by abrupt/non-abrupt thaw, feature category, or source (Alaska Thaw DB / Pan-Arctic Slumps).
permafrost-thaw.limitations: Alaska sub-source is not pan-Arctic; the ARTS sub-source broadens geographic coverage to circumpolar (Siberia, Canada, Eurasia) but covers retrogressive thaw slumps only — the full 9-category taxonomy remains Alaska-only. ARTS points are centroids of digitised slump polygons, not the original footprint. The map shows only the 40,102 slumps ARTS marks as TrainClass=Positive; it omits the 21,269 Negative samples, which ARTS defines as 'background' (non-slump training areas for its detection models). Observed occurrences are unevenly sampled (denser near roads, long-term field sites and accessible regions); absence of points does not mean absence of thaw. Temporal resolution varies (imagery spanning ~70 years).
permafrost-thaw.source: Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.16996415 (Webb et al. 2026, ESSD 18:3147, CC-BY 4.0); whrc/ARTS v6.0.0, Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.10535025 (CC0)

mosaic-sediment.label: Marine Sediment Carbon (MOSAIC)
mosaic-sediment.description: Global synthesis of surficial continental-margin sediment cores compiled by the MOSAIC database (ETH Zürich), covering total organic carbon (TOC), total nitrogen (TN), stable carbon isotopes (δ¹³C), and radiocarbon age (Δ¹⁴C). Complements the Arctic-only CASCADE sediment-carbon layer with global, non-polar coverage.
mosaic-sediment.reading: Select a variable using the layer controls; each dot or hex cell is coloured by its value. δ¹³C indicates whether the carbon is marine- or land-derived; Δ¹⁴C indicates its age (more negative = older, pre-aged carbon). Click a point for the full set of measured values and a link to the original source paper — every value is individually traceable by DOI.
mosaic-sediment.limitations: Continental margins only — the deep abyssal plain and the Arctic Ocean are not the focus of this compilation (see the separate CASCADE layer for Arctic sediment carbon). Radiocarbon (Δ¹⁴C) measurements are far sparser than the other three variables because they are costlier to run. Compiled from many original studies with differing methods and sampling years; not a continuously updated monitoring series.
mosaic-sediment.source: MOSAIC (Modern Ocean Sediment Archive and Inventory of Carbon), Van der Voort et al. 2021, Earth System Science Data 13:2135–2146. ETH Zürich. doi:10.5168/mosaic019.1. Licence: CC-BY 4.0.

ocean-acidification.label: Ocean Acidification (modeled)
ocean-acidification.description: Global field of seawater aragonite (ΩA) and calcite (ΩC) saturation state, on the same hexagon grid as the other carbon-chemistry layers. The Ω fields themselves are GLODAP's own authoritative mapped climatology — not a platform model. What IS platform-derived is the aragonite saturation-horizon depth: the shallowest depth at which ΩA crosses below 1, computed here from GLODAP's 33-depth OmegaA grid. Below Ω = 1, seawater is corrosive to aragonite, the more soluble form of calcium carbonate that many shell- and skeleton-building organisms — pteropods, corals, some plankton — depend on. The horizon is of particular Arctic relevance: cold, low-alkalinity Arctic water shoals the horizon faster than anywhere else, meaning corrosive conditions can already be found at shallower depths there. A sibling variable, the aragonite saturation-horizon shift, shows how many metres shallower the horizon has moved since preindustrial times. It is entirely platform-derived: aragonite saturation is reconstructed with PyCO2SYS from GLODAP's present-day (TCO2) and preindustrial (PI_TCO2) dissolved inorganic carbon, run through one identical CO2SYS configuration for both epochs, and the two resulting horizon depths are then differenced. 'Present-day' here means GLODAP's own mapped reference year (nominally ~2002), not the current calendar year — this compares two climatology snapshots, not a running trend.
ocean-acidification.reading: Click a cell to see ΩA and ΩC at the selected depth, plus the derived saturation-horizon depth and its state (shoaled/typical/deep, or 'always supersaturated' where the horizon does not exist in the water column). The diverging colour ramp reads red (<1, corrosive to aragonite) → white (≈1, the saturation threshold) → blue (>1, supersaturated). The horizon-depth variable is a separate shallow-to-deep map with no depth selector of its own — it already represents a single depth per cell. When the saturation-horizon shift variable is selected, each cell instead reports a single shoaling value in metres — positive means the horizon has moved shallower since preindustrial, i.e. the corrosive zone has expanded upward — again with no depth selector, since it is already one value per cell.
ocean-acidification.limitations: GLODAPv2.2016b is a static mapped climatology, not a real-time measurement — it reflects historical seawater carbon chemistry synthesis, not current conditions. The saturation-horizon depth is linearly interpolated between GLODAP's 33 standard reporting depths, so it is an approximation between sampled levels, not a continuous profile. Cells whose entire water column stays supersaturated (ΩA never crosses below 1) carry no horizon value by design — this is not missing data. Coverage follows GLODAP's mapped ocean domain: finite cells thin with depth (from ~89% of ocean cells at the surface to ~58% at 3000 m) because fewer locations reach those depths — this reflects ocean bathymetry, not a data gap. The saturation-horizon shift is a difference between two static reconstructions, not an observed rate or trend — never read it as metres per year. Cells where either epoch's reconstructed horizon is undefined (no crossing found, or an input field missing) carry no shift value and render blank; a blank cell means 'no shift value available', never 'zero shift'.
ocean-acidification.method: The saturation horizon is derived, not sourced directly: for each hex cell, GLODAP's OmegaA is read at all 33 standard depths, and the shallowest depth at which the value first drops below 1 is located by linear interpolation between the last supersaturated depth and the first undersaturated one. Cells where OmegaA never drops below 1 across the full depth range are flagged as 'always supersaturated' and have no horizon depth. ΩA and ΩC themselves are read directly from the GLODAPv2.2016b mapped climatology with no platform-side modification. The saturation-horizon shift is a second-order derivation built on top of the horizon: for both the present-day and preindustrial epochs, aragonite saturation state is reconstructed with PyCO2SYS from GLODAP's dissolved inorganic carbon (TCO2 for present-day, PI_TCO2 for preindustrial) using one identical CO2SYS configuration; each reconstructed Ω grid is then walked to a saturation-horizon depth exactly as above, and the preindustrial horizon depth is subtracted from the present-day horizon depth. The present-day epoch corresponds to GLODAP's own mapped reference year (nominally ~2002), not the present calendar year, so the shift is the difference between two fixed climatology snapshots, not a per-year rate.
ocean-acidification.source: GLODAP v2.2016b Mapped Climatology (OmegaA/OmegaC). Horizon depth platform-derived. Saturation-horizon shift additionally reconstructed via PyCO2SYS from GLODAP's TCO2/PI_TCO2 fields; platform-derived, referenced to GLODAP's mapped year (~2002).

coral-acid-exposure.label: Coral Acidification Exposure (modeled)
coral-acid-exposure.description: Crosses this platform's own VME coral-suitability model with the aragonite saturation horizon from the Ocean Acidification layer, on the same hexagon grid used across the carbon-chemistry layers. For every hexagon the VME model has already scored, this layer samples the GEBCO 2024 seafloor depth and reads two reconstructed aragonite saturation-horizon depths — present-day and preindustrial — then classifies the cell by where the seabed sits relative to both. Four states, most-alarming first: newly corrosive (the seabed was above the horizon, i.e. supersaturated, before industrialisation, but sits below it today), corrosive before industrialisation (the seabed was already below the horizon before 1850), supersaturated (the seabed sits above both horizons), and no data (seafloor depth, either horizon, or the coral-suitability score is missing at that cell). This is EXPOSURE, not loss: a corrosive reading means the water at that seabed is undersaturated with respect to aragonite. Cold-water corals are documented living below the saturation horizon and calcifying at a metabolic cost — a corrosive cell is not evidence that coral there is dead, absent, or doomed.
coral-acid-exposure.reading: Click a cell to see its exposure state, GEBCO seafloor depth, the two reconstructed aragonite horizon depths (today and preindustrial), and the VME suitability score at that location. Below the per-cell readout, a regional summary reports the suitability-weighted share of modeled coral habitat exposed to any corrosive water, and the share that became corrosive only since preindustrial times, alongside a threshold-sensitivity table showing how those shares move at increasing suitability cutoffs (≥0.3, ≥0.5, ≥0.7) — so the headline is never the answer of one arbitrarily chosen threshold. Colours follow the four states, most-alarming first: magenta (newly corrosive), muted purple (corrosive before industrialisation), blue (supersaturated), slate (no data).
coral-acid-exposure.limitations: Both inputs feeding this layer are modeled, not observed. Coral habitat comes from this platform's own MaxEnt VME suitability model (current published skill: AUC 0.875, Boyce 0.518) — its own biases (uneven DSCRTP survey effort, extrapolation outside the sampled environmental range) carry through here; see the VME Suitability layer's own limitations for detail. The aragonite saturation horizons come from a 1°×1° GLODAPv2.2016b climatology, linearly interpolated between 33 standard depths — an approximation between sampled levels, not a continuous profile. 'Today' means GLODAP's own mapped reference year, nominally ~2002, not the current calendar year: this layer compares two fixed climatology snapshots, present-day versus preindustrial, and is NOT a rate or a trend — 'newly corrosive' means 'corrosive by ~2002 but not before 1850', never 'corrosive as of this year'. This is exposure, never loss: a corrosive classification means the seabed sits in undersaturated water, not that coral there is dead, absent, or doomed — cold-water corals are documented calcifying below the saturation horizon at a metabolic cost. A hexagon missing any input — seafloor depth, either horizon, or the suitability score — is classified no_data and excluded from every summary statistic, never counted as exposed or unexposed. Seabed substrate (Dutkiewicz et al. 2015, CC-BY-NC) enters this layer only INDIRECTLY, as one of six predictors inside the upstream VME suitability model — it is not read or shown directly here.
coral-acid-exposure.method: For every hexagon already scored by the VME suitability model, this layer samples the GEBCO 2024 seafloor depth and both reconstructed aragonite saturation-horizon depths (present-day and preindustrial, from the Ocean Acidification layer's own PyCO2SYS reconstruction) at the cell's centroid, then classifies the cell purely from where the seabed sits relative to the two horizons: at or above the present-day horizon → supersaturated; below the present-day horizon but at or above the preindustrial horizon → newly corrosive; below both → corrosive before industrialisation. A horizon of 'never crosses Ω=1' (an always-supersaturated water column) is treated as infinitely deep, so a seabed can never be classified newly corrosive against it. Any missing input — seafloor depth, either horizon, or a VME suitability score for the cell — yields no_data rather than a guess. The regional summary weights each classified cell by its own continuous VME suitability score (never a hard habitat/non-habitat cutoff) when computing the exposed and newly-exposed shares, then repeats the computation restricted to cells at increasing suitability cutoffs to show how sensitive the headline is to that choice.

dataSources.name: NOAA DSCRTP — coral occurrences (VME model training)
Dutkiewicz et al. 2015 — seabed substrate (indirect VME predictor)

coral-acid-exposure.source: Platform-derived analysis crossing our own MaxEnt VME coral-suitability model (modeled, not observed) with aragonite saturation horizons reconstructed via PyCO2SYS from GLODAP v2.2016b present-day and preindustrial dissolved inorganic carbon. Seabed substrate (Dutkiewicz et al. 2015, CC-BY-NC) enters indirectly as one VME predictor. Exposure to undersaturated water — NOT a prediction of habitat loss.

cumulative-human-impact.label: Cumulative Human Impact (modelled)
cumulative-human-impact.description: A modelled, dimensionless index of total human pressure on marine ecosystems (NCEAS / Halpern et al. 2025) — the present-state sum of roughly ten anthropogenic stressors across six categories (climate, fishing, land-based pollution, shipping, and more), rendered on the same hexagon grid as the other ocean-field layers. It is a synthesis index, not a measurement of any single activity. Crucially, seabed mining is only a minor component of the total, and ISA exploration-claim areas sit in relatively low-impact abyssal zones. This layer is context, not accusation: a concession polygon is not a causal source of this impact. Present-state only — no future projection in this version. Source data are public domain (CC0 1.0).
cumulative-human-impact.reading: Click a cell to read its dimensionless cumulative-impact value. Higher values mean greater total human pressure. The sequential colour ramp runs calm deep-teal (low pressure, most of the open ocean) → cyan → warm amber → deep red (concentrated coastal and high-traffic hotspots). Switch between the Field view (a smooth raster) and the Hexagons view (a pickable grid that returns the exact value on click). There is no depth or variable selector — this is a single surface index per cell.
cumulative-human-impact.limitations: A modelled index, not an observation. It combines stressor layers of differing resolution, vintage and certainty into one dimensionless number, so absolute values are only meaningful in relative terms — read patterns, not decimals. It reflects the study's present-state reference, not the current year, and carries no trend or rate information. Seabed mining contributes only marginally to the total; do NOT read a high or low value over an ISA claim as evidence about mining. A concession polygon is not a causal source of this impact, and an absent value is land or no-data, not zero pressure.
cumulative-human-impact.source: NCEAS / Halpern et al. 2025, 'Cumulative impacts to global marine ecosystems' (Science, doi:10.1126/science.adv2906). Data archived on the KNB repository (doi:10.5063/F18K77KZ), CC0 1.0 Public Domain. Present-state cumulative-impact index; a modelled synthesis, not a measurement. Seabed mining is a minor component — context, not accusation.

ais-live.label: Live Vessels (AIS)
ais-live.description: Raw AIS positions broadcast by ships, from AISStream.io — the last ~60 minutes. Each dot is one vessel; click for name, flag, type, speed and destination.
ais-live.reading: Colour encodes broad ship class. A dense coastal stream is normal; open-ocean gaps are expected on the free tier.
ais-live.limitations: Free-tier AIS coverage is coastal/nearshore only — open-ocean areas including ISA lease waters are out of AIS scope. Positions are as-broadcast; a ship with AIS off is invisible here (see Dark Vessels).

vessel-events.label: Dark Vessels
vessel-events.description: SAR×AIS detections: vessels seen in Sentinel-1 radar imagery matched against AIS. Red = dark (radar detection with no AIS), green = matched, amber = ambiguous.
vessel-events.reading: A red marker is a radar contact with no corresponding AIS broadcast in the correlation window — a candidate 'dark' vessel, not proof of wrongdoing.
vessel-events.limitations: Coverage is coastal only and depends on a recent Sentinel-1 pass. A detection is only 'dark' where other vessels' AIS was received within 50 km / ±1 h; otherwise it is 'ambiguous' (coverage gap). Absence of markers means no recent scene, not an empty sea.

marhys.label: Vent Fluid Chemistry (MARHYS)
marhys.description: Measured compositions of marine hydrothermal vent fluids — a global compilation of 6,788 samples from 153 vent areas, drawn from the published literature and released as MARHYS Database 4.0 (Diehl & Bach 2024). Each point is one sample at the coordinates the source published. Three kinds of sample sit in the dataset and are coloured apart: fluid measured at a vent (HF), an end-member composition extrapolated from it (EM), and background seawater collected as a reference (SW).
marhys.reading: points = individual samples, colour = sample type (orange = vent fluid, red = end-member, blue = background seawater); click one for its full composition, collection metadata and the sparse tail of rarer parameters; switch to Density to see where sampling clusters. ⚠️ A magnesium reading of 0 is a real value, not a gap — an end-member composition is defined by extrapolation to zero magnesium.
marhys.limitations: 883 of the 6,788 samples cannot be placed on the map and are absent from it: 844 carry no usable coordinate, and 39 Guaymas Basin samples carry a latitude of 111.4°, which no latitude can be — the source transposed its two axes and lost the longitude's minus sign. Those rows are stored with the source's own numbers and no geometry; nothing is repaired. One further sample is misplaced but renders anyway: MARHYS puts the Saldanha Hydrothermal Field at 36.567 / +33.6, which GEBCO 2020 places 417 m above sea level in Turkey, where InterRidge has 36.567 / −33.433. It is the only one of 811 MARHYS positions that lands on dry ground. The collection date is free text in eight different formats (year only, month and year, ranges, lists) and is shown exactly as written rather than parsed into a date. Coverage follows the published literature, so it is dense at long-studied fields (East Pacific Rise, Mid-Atlantic Ridge) and thin elsewhere — absence of a sample is not absence of a vent. The dataset is frozen at version 4.0 behind its DOI and is not updated.
marhys.sources: MARHYS Database 4.0 — Diehl, Alexander; Bach, Wolfgang (2024), PANGAEA, doi:10.1594/PANGAEA.972999, CC-BY-4.0 (download.pangaea.de/dataset/972999). The dataset's own terms require the base publication to be cited alongside it: Diehl, A. & Bach, W. (2020), MARHYS (MARine HYdrothermal Solutions) Database: A Global Compilation of Marine Hydrothermal Vent Fluid, End-Member, and Seawater Compositions, Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems, doi:10.1029/2020GC009385. Compiled at MARUM, University of Bremen.

howto.nav_clickClaim: open detailed popup with contractor info, species, Argo floats, and vent conflicts
howto.nav_shiftclick: pin a second popup near the click without closing the current one; repeat to compare multiple locations side by side
howto.sidebar_toggles: show or hide each data layer; toggled-off layers are dimmed. Choices persist across sessions.
howto.sidebar_locate: flies the map to that layer's data, cycling through features one by one. Respects active filters: Argo cycles through alarm-matching floats only; OBIS Species (Deep) cycles through IUCN-filtered species only; Hydrothermal Vents cycles through status-filtered vents only.
howto.sidebar_claimRisk: filter Mining Concessions by risk type (biodiversity overlap, Argo nearby, vent conflict, UNESCO proximity); collapsed by default
howto.sidebar_ventStatus: show or hide confirmed-active, inferred-active, and inactive vents independently; collapsed by default
howto.sidebar_iucnFilter: expand OBIS Species (Deep) to filter by IUCN Red List category (CR, EN, VU, NT, LC). Only observations matching selected categories are shown on the map.
howto.sidebar_alarmFilter: show only Argo floats matching one or more alarm types; collapsed by default. A badge shows the count of active alarms.
howto.sidebar_contractors: toggle individual operators on/off; collapsed by default
howto.sidebar_reset: appears in the panel header whenever any filter is active; clears all filters in one tap
howto.sidebar_mobile: tap the map or open a detail popup to auto-close the sidebar
howto.iucn_green: Not threatened or not yet evaluated
howto.iucn_note: At low zoom, each dot summarizes a geographic cell. At high zoom (zoom 8+), each dot is one species observation. Use the IUCN Filter in the Layers panel to show only species of a specific threat level.
howto.risk_high: active vent inside active Polymetallic Sulphide concession
howto.risk_conflict: active vent inside any active concession
howto.risk_dormant: inactive vent inside a concession (may still host endemic fauna)
howto.risk_historical: inactive vent, concession is inactive or relinquished
howto.noise_intro: Enable the Noise Risk Grid layer to see underwater acoustic impact cells across the OSPAR/HELCOM/Baltic region and global EMODnet monitoring stations. Each cell represents a 1° × 1° grid square (~111 km per side).
howto.noise_critical: severe noise combined with high cetacean density and/or threatened species weight
howto.noise_high: elevated noise with significant cetacean presence
howto.noise_low: noise measured but limited cetacean impact
howto.noise_datagap: high noise detected but no cetacean survey data available for this cell
howto.noise_filter: Use the Risk Level filter (+) in the sidebar to show only cells above a specific threshold — e.g. select Critical + High to focus on the most acoustically stressed areas. The zoom button (⊙) cycles through filtered cells.
howto.noise_mining: When you open a Mining Concession popup, nearby noise risk cells (within 200 km) are listed in the panel — showing whether the claim lies in an already acoustically compromised area. Mining would add impulsive noise on top of existing industrial sources.
howto.chess_intro: Enable the Chemosynthetic Sites layer to see cold seeps, whale falls, and oxygen-minimum zone communities from the ChEssBase dataset (served via GBIF).
howto.chess_filter: Filter by habitat type (seep / whale fall / OMZ) or by phylum (Annelida, Mollusca, etc.) using the + button in the layers menu.
howto.chess_vents: Hydrothermal vents with nearby ChEssBase records show a species count badge in their popup. Click Generate Vent Report for a full species table and nearby claim analysis.
howto.argo_intro: Enable the Argo layer, then expand it in the sidebar to reveal four alarm checkboxes. Activating one or more hides all floats that do not match any selected alarm — so only anomalous floats remain visible.
howto.argo_oxygen: O₂ below the depth-adaptive threshold (see Alarm Filters tab for exact values)
howto.argo_temp: surface temperature more than 2 standard deviations from the current dataset mean
howto.argo_salinity: surface salinity more than 2 σ from the dataset mean
howto.argo_logic: Multiple alarms use OR logic — a float is shown if it triggers any of the selected alarms. The zoom (⊙) button in the sidebar only cycles through currently visible floats.
howto.drift_trail: Each Argo float shows a lime-green trail (or red if any sensor alarm is active) connecting up to 180 days of surfacing events. Dots mark each past position.
howto.drift_track: Click any Argo float and press "Track all drift plumes" to back-trace ocean currents from every recorded position using Copernicus Marine (CMEMS) data at 1,000 m depth. Magenta lines show where water masses originated 7 days before each measurement.
howto.drift_clickable: Once plumes are tracked, the trail dots become clickable — tap a dot to see the depth, temperature, salinity, and oxygen measured at that historical position. This helps compare how ocean conditions changed along the float's drift path.
howto.land_intro: The platform includes a parallel set of land-based environmental layers for analysing terrestrial mining impacts. These are off by default — enable them from the welcome screen or the sidebar.
howto.land_footprints: 74k+ mine polygons from satellite imagery. Enable alongside KBAs to see mines inside biodiverse areas.
howto.land_kba: Key Biodiversity Areas (scientific designation) and Protected Areas (legal designation). Layering both reveals which critical biodiversity sites lack legal protection.
howto.land_tailings: 11,587 tailings facilities (WAPHA). Global Tailings Portal hazard classification is withdrawn pending permission. Enable Landslides to find dams in slope-unstable terrain.
howto.land_fires: near-real-time fire detections and government air monitoring. Use together to find fires near mines and track pollution levels at nearby communities.
howto.land_dams: river barriers and satellite-tracked water bodies. Cross-reference with Mining Footprints to trace contamination pathways from mines to downstream water supplies.
howto.land_note: Land layers use the same click-to-inspect, layer-toggle, and locate (⊙) patterns as ocean layers.

alarms.intro: Depth-adaptive thresholds — independent of location, season, or loaded dataset.

lowOxygen.title: Low Oxygen (O₂)
lowOxygen.description: Dissolved oxygen at max dive depth. Normal levels depend on depth — the OMZ is naturally depleted.

lowPh.title: Low pH (Acidification)
lowPh.description: Deep water naturally more acidic from CO₂ accumulation. Thresholds calibrated per depth zone.

usage.title: Usage
usage.step1: Enable the <1>Argo Floats</1> layer in the left sidebar.
usage.step2: Click the <1>Alarm Filter</1> toggle under Argo Floats to expand the alarm checkboxes.
usage.step3: Check one or more alarms. Floats not matching any selected alarm disappear from the map.
usage.step4: Use the <1>⊙</1> locate button to cycle through only the visible (filtered) floats.
usage.step5: Click a float to see exact O₂, pH, temperature, and depth values in the popup.
usage.step6: Multiple alarm types use <1>OR logic</1> — a float is shown if it triggers any selected alarm.
usage.step7: Note: O₂ and pH alarms only flag floats with those sensors (BGC Argo). Most core floats lack these sensors, so those filters may show few or no results.

dates.mining_expiry: The contract end date as published by the ISA. A future date means the contract is still active. ISA contracts are typically 15-year exploration licences.
dates.obis_obs: The date the species was physically observed, from the original OBIS record. This is when the survey happened — not when we fetched it. Historical records (1800s–1990s) reflect the same species being present; absence of recent records does not mean the species is gone.
dates.argo_profile: The date of the last transmitted oceanographic profile. Argo floats surface every ~10 days to transmit. The float may have drifted significantly since this date. The trail shows up to 180 days of past positions.
dates.vents: No date shown — vent data is from the static InterRidge 2020 catalogue. Status (active, confirmed / active, inferred / inactive) is as of the last survey reported to InterRidge; some vents may not have been revisited for decades.
dates.eez: No date shown — EEZ boundaries are political/legal designations. They change only when states formally renegotiate maritime agreements or when ICJ/ITLOS rulings redraw borders. The dataset is World EEZ v12 (2023); major boundaries are stable for years at a time.
dates.unesco: No date shown — UNESCO designations are permanent international recognitions. New sites are added by UNESCO's World Heritage Committee (typically once per year at the annual session); sites are rarely delisted.
dates.oceansites: The "Obs time" in the popup is the timestamp of the reading itself, not the time we fetched it. Which source supplied it is named in the popup and it changes what the timestamp means: NDBC buoys report hourly or better, PMEL ERDDAP is a daily quality-controlled product that lags by days to weeks, and the OceanSITES GDAC is a file archive that lags further still. The "Cached" date below is our own refresh — daily. Most stations in the register carry no observation at all, because only currently operational moorings are polled.
dates.onc: The timestamp shown is when the sensor value was recorded at the instrument, not when we cached it. ONC cable observatories transmit continuously; our daily cache captures the most recent reading. Deep-sea nodes typically have data within hours of measurement. The panel also shows a 72-hour sparkline per sensor, a depth-resolved ADCP mean-backscatter heatmap (last 24 h, in dB, with bin depths in metres), the latest CTD cast profile, and nearby earthquakes (M≥3, 200 km radius, last 30 days) — all sourced from the ONC Oceans 3.0 API and USGS FDSN, refreshed every 4–12 hours.
dates.cables: The cable routing dataset is static — it shows planned/as-built routes, not real-time cable health. EMODnet updates the dataset periodically as new cables are commissioned; our sync pulls the latest version weekly. ONC observatory cables are updated monthly. OOI RCA routes are re-derived quarterly from the oceanobservatories/asset-management GitHub repo — geometry is approximate (straight-line between published Primary Node coordinates; the actual cable follows bathymetry-driven paths that OOI does not publish in machine-readable form).
dates.oncInstruments_title: ONC Instruments — No per-device date shown
dates.oncInstruments: The instrument catalogue records deployment metadata (device category, model, depth) not a live reading. The catalogue is re-synced daily at 00:15 Europe/Warsaw from the ONC Oceans 3.0 WFS. A device appearing in this layer does not necessarily mean it is actively recording — consult the ONC Data Search portal for live status.
dates.ports: Port infrastructure changes slowly; the dataset is a static compiled snapshot. No opening/closure date is tracked. Re-synced monthly from the source repository to catch any corrections.
dates.tectonic: Peter Bird's 2003 plate model is a geological reference dataset, not a time-series. Plate boundary positions are effectively permanent on human timescales. No sync needed; imported once.
dates.chess: ChEssBase records are grouped by named locality; no per-record date is shown. The dataset represents the cumulative body of published literature on chemosynthetic ecosystems — some records date back to the 1970s. Absence of recent records does not mean the ecosystem has disappeared; seeps and whale falls persist for decades.
dates.worms: Species names resolved to canonical WoRMS AphiaIDs; refreshed weekly and on each species sync.
dates.landMining: Polygons are derived from Sentinel-2 imagery collected 2019–2022. No per-feature date — the entire dataset represents a snapshot of mining extent during that window. New mines opened after 2022 are not included.
dates.kba: KBA boundaries reflect the latest assessment published by BirdLife/KBA Partnership. Some sites were first assessed in the 2000s; boundaries are periodically revised. The designation year in the popup shows when the site was first confirmed.
dates.fires: The acquisition date and time in UTC, exactly as NASA publishes them for that overpass. Detections are near-real-time — typically within 3 hours of the satellite pass. The three VIIRS satellites together give several passes a day. A detection is a single observation, not an estimate of how long the fire burned.
dates.airQuality: Pollutant readings show the time of the most recent measurement cached from the source network. Readings are refreshed every 2 hours. If a station shows a reading from several days ago, the station may be offline.
dates.landslides: The date the landslide occurred (or was reported). Older events (2007–2015) may have only a year or month; recent events often have exact dates. Event dates are from news reports or government agencies — there may be a delay of days to weeks between occurrence and cataloguing.
dates.staticDams_title: Tailings Dams, Dams, Surface Water — No live dates
dates.staticDams: These are static or slowly-updated datasets. Tailings data is the static WAPHA compilation (2023) — Global Tailings Portal disclosure fields are withdrawn pending permission. Dam data is a compiled snapshot. Surface Water is a 37-year composite (1984–2021) — it doesn't show current water level.
